## RADD-aitbetjb: expected_failures.txt with a bidirectional rot check

**Status:** done | **Parent:** vsthdwxndzkdtbikhhcrjosjpqtfzqlg

### Description

The harness must flag UNEXPECTED SUCCESSES and leftover unmatched entries, not just failures.

### Comments

#### 2026-07-28 — 142225707+bart-turczynski@users.noreply.github.com

Groundwork landed in RADD-xdgfyznt (ea07fb1). Three things that change how this ticket should be approached:

1. THE CORPUS IS ALREADY DERIVED AND CLASSIFIED. tests/testthat/fixtures/wpt-hosts.csv has an expect column with values ipv4 / ipv6 / regname / url-failure, computed from WPT's OUTPUT rather than its failure flag. The 267 expected failures are not a flat list -- some fail on the host, some on the port or scheme. http://[1::2]:3:4 is the exhibit: WPT fails it, its host 1::2 is well formed, and raddr correctly reads it. Any expected_failures.txt that treats failure as a host verdict will be wrong on that row and on whatever joins it.

2. A ONE-CLASS VERSION OF THE ROT CHECK IS ALREADY RUNNING. test-wpt.R asserts that raddr declines every non-percent-encoded url-failure row except an exactly-pinned exception set, currently that single row out of 69. It catches both directions today -- a row leaving the set means raddr started rejecting a good host, a row entering it means raddr started accepting a bad one. What it does NOT have is this ticket's third requirement: leftover unmatched entries. Generalizing it means covering the 371 authorities the extractor refuses and the 6 percent-encoded rows, both currently excluded with reasons.

3. WHY IT MATTERS MORE THAN IT LOOKS. A mutation run proved the success rows catch almost nothing: widening the final part's bound past 255 and the hex width past 8 digits both survived every success-side assertion, because under a widened rule both sides of the comparison are still addresses. The rows that must NOT parse are where the discriminating power lives. This ticket owns most of them.

#### 2026-07-28 — 142225707+bart-turczynski@users.noreply.github.com

Done, three commits on feature/wpt-corpus (150b309, 8e66419, 9f01320). Recorded in docs/architecture.md section 11.8.

WHAT LANDED. tests/testthat/fixtures/expected_failures.txt, four classes: reads-failed-url (WPT failed the URL, raddr reads the host, 1 row), declines-pct-encoded (WPT reached an address, raddr declines because the URL parser decoded first, 2 rows), format-divergence (same address, different text, 1 row), extractor-refusal (5 rules over 371 rows). Each class states a DIRECTION and the direction is checked, so a misfiled row does not buy the same exemption for free.

THE THIRD DIRECTION, which is the ticket's point. Regression, unexpected success and leftover are three separate expectations rather than one set comparison, because they call for opposite actions -- fix the parser, delete the entry, notice the row is gone. Rows are keyed by (source, input) and never by index: an index shifts under any upstream insertion, so an index key turns one re-sync into 128 leftovers and teaches everyone to ignore the check.

THE UNPLANNED STRENGTHENING. The suite used to drop all six percent-encoded rows on the pct_encoded column. Only two actually turn on the decode; the other four were getting a free pass, and nothing would have caught raddr starting to read http://[::%31] as an address. Listing two by name puts four back under assertion. 69 url-failure rows to 72, with no exceptions left inline.

THE 371 REFUSALS. vendor-wpt.R now attributes each to a named rule and writes tests/testthat/fixtures/wpt-refusals.csv; --check re-derives and diffs it; the suite holds the hand-written account against that table both ways. A fixture, not a provenance field, because data-raw/ is .Rbuildignore'd and absent under R CMD check. Counts: no-authority 333, pre-parse-removal 23, backslash-authority 8, multiple-colons 4, ambiguous-userinfo 3. multiple-colons is the expensive one -- http://2001::1 and http://2001::1] are unbracketed IPv6 that WHATWG must reject, exactly the shape raddr's gate has to get right. Worth a follow-up if the file ever grows a way to state an expected host token by hand.

--check also stopped spot-checking the provenance: three fields to every generated field, from one definition shared with the write path.

MEASURED BY BREAKING IT. Eight perturbations, all caught, each naming its own fault: deleted entry, entry for a row that agrees, entry pointing at a row that is gone, wrong direction, mistyped class, hand-edited refusal count, dropped refusal rule, unparseable line. The run found a defect in the check itself -- the class vocabulary was asserted set-equal, which would have gone red the day someone FIXED the last divergence in a class and removed its entry. One-directional now. It also caught one of my own entries on the first run: the v4-mapped divergence filed under wpt when the row is one of raddr's own additions.

VERIFY. lintr clean; R CMD check --as-cran 0 errors / 0 warnings / 1 pre-existing NOTE; both staleness guards in sync; wpt suite 42 assertions over 9 tests, was 30. The derived corpus CSV is byte-identical to before, so none of this moved the corpus.

Push still blocked (403, account suspended); 51 local commits unpushed.

## RADD-blpcanps: O6b — does glibc/musl getaddrinfo do the scope lift, now that addr_curl() inherits it

**Status:** done | **Parent:** pbwpleuzfntiksjhkjicnjrgyxkthhqd

### Description

RADD-puzhycev moved addr_curl()'s fallback from bare pton to the addr_getaddrinfo() entry point, which means Apple's KAME-reverse scope lift (section 3.5.3) is now part of curl's IPv6 reading. Before the fix addr_curl() was lift-free.

That widens the platform-varying surface, and O6 (RADD-xrgomyhx) does not cover it. O6 is scoped to section 3.3's pton column -- IPv4 -- and asks whether glibc shows the same pton-then-aton boundary. It does not ask whether glibc's or musl's getaddrinfo lifts an embedded scope out of fe80::/10 at all.

The question: if glibc does NOT lift, then on Linux curl reads fe80:abcd::1 as fe80:abcd::1 -- which is exactly the answer raddr just stopped giving. addr_curl() and addr_getaddrinfo() would be Apple-only for the whole of fe80::/10, not just for a boundary detail, and section 3.1's stability column would need to say so (it currently marks only pton platform-varying, and section 5's default-dialect argument leans on that wording).

The fold was already re-measured through PHP's inet_pton [verified 2026-07-27], which ruled out the Python binding as the source and pinned it to libc -- but that was the fold, not the lift, and both were Apple only.

Probe: Docker with a glibc and a musl image, run data-raw/oracle-ipv6.py's getaddrinfo half, diff the gai_scope column against the recorded fixture. Same instrument caveats as RADD-xpmuxafb: let DNS work and check the resolver is honest instead.

If it differs by platform that is a finding worth recording in section 3.5.3's table, and possibly worth reporting upstream.

### Comments

#### 2026-07-29 — 142225707+bart-turczynski@users.noreply.github.com

Settled 2026-07-29, commit d26fc63, in the same Docker pass as RADD-xrgomyhx. The answer is the worst case this issue was filed to check for: glibc and musl getaddrinfo do NOT lift.

fe80:abcd::1 stays fe80:abcd::1 at scope 0 on both. With an explicit %lo the scope is set to 1 and the second hextet is STILL left standing. Apple gives fe80::1 at scope 43981. Verified identical on glibc 2.36 and musl 1.2.5.

So the prediction in the description holds exactly: on Linux curl reads fe80:abcd::1 as fe80:abcd::1, which is the answer raddr stopped giving under RADD-puzhycev. addr_getaddrinfo() and addr_curl() are Apple readings for the WHOLE of fe80::/10, not for a boundary detail. Outside the block the platforms agree, so the divergence is bounded by fe80::/10 and not by the dialect -- asserted in test-libc.R.

Two further findings the probe turned up:
- Linux inet_pton takes NO zone ID at all. Any literal with a % is rejected, %lo and %1 alike. So section 5.1's fold cannot arise there either, and the fold is Apple-only for a second reason on top of the interface-table one.
- Linux getaddrinfo accepts a zone only on a SCOPED address (link-local, multicast); 2001:db8::1%lo, ::1%lo and 1:2:3:4:5:6:7:8%lo are rejections. And the name must resolve -- %bogus0 and wrong-case %LO are rejections where Apple reports scope 0.

The instrument caveat in the description was real and bit: the IPv6 corpus spells its zones %lo0/%en0, which are Apple names, so in a container every zone row rejects because the loopback is lo. That would have been read as a glibc finding when it measured the container's interface table. data-raw/oracle-zone-native.py substitutes each host's own names from if_nameindex() and is what the findings above rest on.

Doc: new section 3.5.3.1 records it. The lift's justification survives -- 'pure arithmetic on the input' is still why raddr MAY model the lift while it may not model the fold -- but it was never why raddr SHOULD, and 3.5.3.1 now says so: the transform is a function of the input, but whether a platform applies it at all is not.

## RADD-bxjyndha: Nothing guarded the en-US claim; wire spelling into the verify hook

**Status:** done | **Parent:** yrppvxdipdzfceotkqiaqeoqcjfcvqof

### Description

Follow-up to RADD-oekxupgo, which fixed 11 British spellings but left the hole open: the package had no spelling dependency and no inst/WORDLIST, so spell_check_package() flagged all 82 domain terms and could not be used as a gate.

Done:
- inst/WORDLIST generated via spelling::update_wordlist(), 77 words. That is exactly the 82 minus the 5 British spellings oekxupgo fixed, which is a useful cross-check that the fix was complete. Every entry reviewed by hand: acronyms (IANA, LACNIC, WHATWG, CIDR), RFC terms of art (hextet, unicast, forwardable), package names (vctrs, bignum, testthat), tool/libc names (glibc, musl, PCRE's), and coined words (digitless, decapsulators). No typo was whitelisted.
- spelling added to Suggests.
- tests/spelling.R with error = TRUE, skip_on_cran = TRUE.
- The verify hook in .pre-commit-config.yaml now calls spelling::spell_check_package() and quits 1 on any flagged word, in the same shape as the existing lint step.

WHY THE HOOK AND NOT JUST THE TEST FILE, which is the whole point of this issue: skip_on_cran = TRUE early-returns unless NOT_CRAN is one of 1/yes/true, and rcmdcheck is called with env = character() while callr::rcmd_safe_env() does not set NOT_CRAN either. Verified both. So the stock spelling setup would have been INERT under this project's own gate — a guard that never runs where it matters. The explicit hook step removes the dependency on NOT_CRAN semantics entirely.

Verification, all three paths measured with a deliberate 'mispelng' in a vignette:
- verify hook: exit 1, prints 'mispelng edge-cases.Rmd:304'.
- tests/spelling.R with NOT_CRAN=true: exit 1, 'Potential spelling errors: mispelng'.
- tests/spelling.R with NOT_CRAN unset: exit 0, inert, which is the intended CRAN posture since a hunspell or dictionary difference there would fail the check for a reason no edit could fix.

Gate green after the change: 0 lints, 0 flagged words, 0 errors, 0 warnings, 1 note. spelling.R runs inside R CMD check without failing.

#### 2026-07-28 — 142225707+bart-turczynski@users.noreply.github.com

Scope gap: this ticket names sitemapr and robotstxtr, but rurl is the largest
in-house consumer and the only one carrying its own IP code. Measured today
(both repos, no code changed):

WHERE raddr WINS OUTRIGHT -- the WHATWG reading. rurl's hand-rolled
.parse_whatwg_ipv4_host() and addr_whatwg() agree exactly: 20/21 on a first
corpus, 31/31 targeted, plus a 99-case sweep. The single divergence is
::ffff:0:0/96 rendering, and it is not blocking -- a ~20-line serializer over
the EXPORTED addr_to_bytes() reproduces rurl's WHATWG output 18/18 including
first-run-wins compression. rurl can delegate its WHATWG IPv4 reading.

WHERE THE LAYERS DIVERGE -- and this is the thing to decide. rurl's
R/parse-web.R is a CURLU (URL-host) reproduction, calibrated per-octet against
real libcurl. addr_curl() is 'aton falling back to pton' -- the RESOLVER layer.
Both correct about their own layer. Differential run today against real libcurl
8.14.1:

  host           libcurl 8.14.1   rurl .web_ipv4_normalize   addr_curl()
  0Xff           0Xff (name)      0Xff (name)                0.0.0.255
  192.0.048.1    192.0.048.1      192.0.048.1 (name)         192.0.48.1
  4294967296     4294967296       4294967296 (name)          0.0.0.0
  1.2.3.4 junk   -                (name)                     1.2.3.4
  0x, 1.2.3.4.   name             name                       NA (agrees)

rurl vs real libcurl: 13/13 agree. So rurl's calibration is sound and
addr_curl() is answering a different question -- exactly as its own docs say
('the whole reason 192.0.048.1 reaches a host under curl that a browser refuses
to dial'). Uppercase 0X is a discriminator worth adding to the fixtures either
way: CURLU rejects it, inet_aton accepts it.

ALSO NOT DELEGABLE: the host/address boundary. raddr has no reg-name concept.
0xg, 0x1p, ..., ., .. are rurl correctly returning reg-name via
.host_ends_in_number_vec(). Ungated delegation turns valid hosts into parse
failures on a CRAN package.

CONSEQUENCE FOR THE ROADMAP: RADD-xdgfyznt already vendors WPT urltestdata.json
(43 numeric-IPv4 authorities, 44 bracketed IPv6), which is URL-layer material --
so raddr's WHATWG side is heading to the URL layer anyway. There is no
equivalent for curl on either roadmap. Whether raddr grows a URL-host-layer
curl dialect is what decides if rurl's R/parse-web.R can ever be retired;
without it, rurl keeps that file regardless of how good addr_whatwg() is.

rurl side tracked at RURL-cbrfphfr.

Done, two commits: 69700f2 (test-migration.R + the helper move) and 4383d5c (architecture section 11.10). Measured READ-ONLY in all three repos; nothing changed in any of them.

SCOPE FINDING FIRST, because it reframes the ticket. THE TWO GUARDS ARE ONE
IMPLEMENTATION. sitemapr's and robotstxtr's R/ssrf.R are byte-identical for the
whole IP body -- 232 lines, 11 functions -- differing only in the entry point
(ssrf_check_parsed takes a parsed rurl row, robots_ssrf_check takes a URL). So
'run both guards' assertions' is running one guard's assertions twice, their
agreement with each other is evidence of nothing, and a defect in one is a
defect in both. That duplication is a stronger argument for delegating than any
divergence below.

rurl was NOT touched. RURL-cbrfphfr carries an owner decision of 2026-07-28 --
'do no further IP work in rurl, let raddr ship then consume it' -- and is
hard-blocked on a raddr release anyway (rurl is on CRAN, no HEAD pins). Its
2026-07-28 comment already did the head-to-head, so re-running it would have
been redundant.

AGREEMENT IS THE NULL RESULT, AND IT IS THE HEADLINE. raddr's 1861-literal
hostile corpus through the guard: 659 literals read by both, ZERO
disagreements on the bits. And zero literals raddr reads that the guard
refuses -- so delegation cannot loosen the guard, which is the direction that
matters for a security control. Three literals go the other way, and they are
two different findings.

FINDING 1 (filed RADD-sytkadrv): the guard's fail-closed posture has a
trailing-separator hole. '::1:', '::ffff:', '1:2:3:4:5:6:7:8:' and '1.2.3.4.'
all read as valid addresses, because R's strsplit() drops a trailing empty
field so the arity check passes. This contradicts the guard's own header
invariant, and independence from rurl's pre-validation is what SITE-vovtwvuh
set out to establish. Severity bounded and stated as such on the ticket: it
makes the guard read 'X:' as 'X', so it OVER-accepts rather than under-blocks;
'::1:' still classifies loopback and is still refused. No bypass demonstrated.
raddr calls all three IPv6 forms malformed under every one of the six dialects.

FINDING 2 (not a defect, and worth saying so): the trailing DOT is not the
guard's mistake. '1.2.3.4.' is a hostname carrying the DNS root label -- WHATWG
reads it as an address, the other five dialects refuse, and raddr reports
'divergent' rather than picking a side. The guard agrees with WHATWG silently,
without knowing that is what it is doing. Exactly the P3 case, and the fact it
needs is one raddr already has.

FINDING 3 (filed RADD-jbqmznoz): one reason code is wrong. The guard files
100.64.0.0/10 under 'cloud-metadata'; that is RFC 6598 Shared Address Space
(CGNAT). raddr answers 'shared'. The codes are documented machine-readable and
stable, so a caller keying off cloud-metadata misattributes every CGNAT
address. Smaller sibling: 0.0.0.0/8 filed as 'unspecified' where raddr says
'this_network' -- only 0.0.0.0/32 is unspecified.

WHAT raddr SUPPLIES: every range-derived reason code is a rename of an
addr_category() value (loopback, private, link_local, this_network, shared),
and the entire embedding inventory is addr_embedded_kind() + addr_embeddings(),
both ISATAP markers included. ssrf_numeric_literal_blocked()'s obfuscation grep
is answered structurally instead: a literal the lenient dialects read and
strict refuses IS the obfuscation, and it arrives with the address each dialect
saw. What raddr declines to supply is 'cloud-metadata' and the metadata
hostname -- policy, P8, ssrfr's.

NOTHING CHANGED IN raddr. The diff found no defect in it, and the literals were
already pinned (test-codes.R's trailing_dot, test-ipv6.R's stray-colon block).
test-migration.R pins the CONTRACT instead -- the category vocabulary and the
embedding inventory the migration will rest on -- because no existing test
forced those to stay put.

VERIFICATION: lintr clean; rcmdcheck --as-cran 0 errors 0 warnings 1 NOTE (the
pre-existing one); full suite 1921 assertions over 447 tests, 0 failures, was
1898/440. Push still 403s; 55 commits local.

(2) I described running amd64-under-emulation as 'a feature' because it varies platform and R version at once. That was wrong — it is a confound, and I nearly misread the result because of it.   x <- "1.2.3.4 junk"; p <- addr_parse(x)

  addr_curl(x)                -> 1.2.3.4      addr_reading(p, "curl") -> NA   <-- diverges

compose_dialects(first, second) returns 'first' untouched unless addr_family(first) is NA. So for the record path to return NA, the stored aton field must already read NA by the time the curl branch of composed_reading() (R/parse.R:353) reaches it. composed_reading() computes the gated gai FIRST, via blank_address(field(x, "pton"), gated) and blank_address(field(x, "aton"), gated), and blank_address() is vec_assign(a, at, vec_slice(a, NA_integer_)). It would show only on old R because R's reference-counting semantics differ. This is a genuine correctness bug in a supported code path, worth its own issue regardless of what happens to the floor number.

## RADD-ddxplrdh: Epic E — Formatting (RFC 5952)

**Status:** done | **Parent:** tazdtmvwzachzhvyjfxexfpyhuypyavp

### Description

addr_format canonical and addr_expand fully expanded. RFC 5952 publishes no test vectors — raddr authors its own (O8).

### Comments

#### 2026-07-26 — 142225707+bart-turczynski@users.noreply.github.com

Epic E landed as ed03e2d (local only; git push still 403s on the suspended account).

Two renderers rather than one. addr_format() is RFC 5952 canonical and backs format()/print()/as.character(); addr_expand() is the fully expanded eight-hextet form and stays public, because the canonical form is variable-width by construction and so cannot line up in a column, sort as text, or be prefix-matched.

The mixed form is decided by the family (v6_4in6, decided by the bits), not the spelling, so parse(format(x)) == x holds including the family. The renderer does not assume the ::ffff: prefix.

Implementation is one 8 x n hextet matrix. The zero run comes from a backwards recursion over the eight rows; the leftmost argmax gives RFC 4.2.3's tie-break for free. The run is blanked rather than removed and the pieces joined with ':' regardless, with one sub(':{3,}', '::') collapsing the rest -- so the ragged part stays inside two vectorized calls.

O8 closed: test-format.R authors the vectors by RFC section, with the RFC's own prose examples as rows, pinned by four properties (round-trip, fixed point, equal-renders-equal, vectorized == one-at-a-time).

test-ipv6.R and test-address.R assertions written against the old placeholder now call addr_expand(), so their expected strings are unchanged.

Measured at 1e6: format 1.1x ipaddress for IPv4, 7.5x for IPv6, vs 18x and 41x for parsing the same values -- and with none of the tuning the parsers needed. Recorded in architecture 11.2 as a sharper reading of O1: pure R pays for irregularity, not volume.

Gate: lintr clean, R CMD check --as-cran 0/0/1 (known private-repo URL NOTE), 255 tests.

#### 2026-07-26 — 142225707+bart-turczynski@users.noreply.github.com

Zone-ID survey (020206b). Paper decision stands; the evidence behind it is now much stronger.

data-raw/survey-zone.sh measures eight implementations and reproduces the table. Tally among parsers that return a value: four reject (Rust std, Ruby IPAddr, PHP filter_var, ada/WHATWG URL), two accept and keep (Python .scope_id, Go Zone()), one accepts and loses it. The paper's answer is also the plurality answer -- it stops being a coin toss.

Two bugs found while measuring:

O16 -- R's ipaddress 1.0.3 accepts a zone and silently discards it. ip_address('fe80::1%lo0') is fe80::1; ip_address('fe80::1%lo0%en0%wat') is also fe80::1; no accessor recovers it. Joins O11's list of bugs to file on davidchall/ipaddress. Direct measured support for architecture 5.1's separate zone field.

O15 -- CPython IPv6Address.exploded and .reverse_pointer raise AddressValueError on any address with a scope_id (3.9.6, 3.12.13, 3.14.6). The renderer re-parses str(self) with the zone attached. Epic K (RADD-wysgbyng) inherits this warning for addr_reverse_pointer().

Near miss worth recording: the first draft of the survey read .exploded and reported 'Python rejects every zone' -- a renderer bug masquerading as a grammar difference. oracle-ipv6.py reads .packed and was never affected; confirmed by regenerating the fixture byte for byte on 3.14.6.

## RADD-dtdcaphz: Epic O — Upstream reports: measured, drafted, and unfiled

**Status:** todo

### Description

Container for every raddr finding whose only remaining step is publishing it to a tracker we cannot reach. Created 2026-07-30, deliberately parented at TOP LEVEL rather than under the v0.1 root RADD-tazdtmvw -- same reasoning as RADD-purmngor. Filing bugs against other people's packages must not block raddr's release.

### The definition of done, restated

These five were originally written with 'a FILED report' as the deliverable. That made an external account problem into a blocker on our own tracker, and it measured the wrong thing: raddr does not control davidchall/ipaddress or python/cpython, and it never did.

What raddr controls, and what is therefore the deliverable:

1. The defect is reproduced against the live library, at a named version, on a named platform.
2. The claim is narrowed to what the measurement actually supports -- no normative language the RFC does not license.
3. A duplicate check is done against the upstream tracker.
4. A submission-ready report exists, in git, with its reproducers run and pasted verbatim.

All four hold for all five children, so all five are DONE. Note that (3) was always available: the suspension 403s AUTHENTICATED GitHub access, not reading a public tracker.

### Nothing here was filed

Stated plainly so no future reader mistakes these for submitted reports. As of 2026-07-30, day 10 of the suspension, zero of the five has been posted. The drafts are at docs/upstream-reports/ (committed) and its README carries the submission order.

### THIS EPIC STAYS OPEN as the one live reminder

Its children are done because the finding work is done. The epic is the single thing left to trip over when the account is restored -- which is the point of collapsing six reminders into one.

When that happens:

- START WITH THE CPYTHON COMMENT. It is a comment on python/cpython#88178, NOT a new issue -- that report has been open since 2021 (bpo-44012). It is the most time-sensitive of the five because PR #25824 is approved and dormant, and its output format would turn .reverse_pointer from a loud exception into a malformed ip6.arpa name. Post before it merges.
- The four davidchall/ipaddress reports are independent and can go in any order. They cross-reference each other, so backfill real issue numbers into the sibling links once the first is filed.
- Then backfill the filed URLs into the five children and close this epic.

Maintenance expectation for davidchall/ipaddress: last commit 2025-08-22, with a gap between 2023-12 and 2025-08. Maintained, slowly. A filing that sits is not a filing that failed.



## RADD-dtmpmpct: Nothing pins the URL-parser vs addr_curl() boundary

**Status:** done | **Parent:** rzdchzcswdehavskhjvpmqoqxodvmooy

### Description

RADD-hnczgkcf corrected a docs claim that had drifted false. Nothing would have caught it: no test compares curl's URL parser against addr_curl(), so the boundary between them is asserted only in prose and can rot again silently.

Measured contract worth pinning (curl 8.20.0, 35-host numeric sweep):
- curl's URL parser admits a STRICT SUBSET of addr_curl()
- where both admit, they never disagree on the address
- there is no input the URL parser admits that addr_whatwg() refuses

A data-raw oracle probing CURLU (via --proxy so no DNS) plus a fixture asserting those three invariants would hold it. Note this is a data-raw oracle only, like adaR -- never a runtime dependency.

Deeper design question, probably v0.2: compose_dialects() expresses fallback precedence only. A URL-parser dialect is guard-then-parse -- failing the guard yields 'not an address' rather than the next parser's answer -- which the current composition algebra has no slot for. Related: RADD-cdmoeadr names sitemapr and robotstxtr but not rurl, the only consumer that exercises the gate shape.

### Comments

#### 2026-07-28 — 142225707+bart-turczynski@users.noreply.github.com

This issue was filed on a layer error -- see the retraction on RADD-hnczgkcf. Correcting the premise rather than closing it, because a smaller version of it survives.

WRONG as filed: framing CURLU as the thing addr_curl() should be checked against. curl's effective host handling is CURLU THEN getaddrinfo, and addr_curl() models that composite correctly -- verified end to end with curl -v on 192.0.048.1, 4294967296, 0Xff and 0177.0.0.1, all four matching. f958cfa already pins this properly with a real curl oracle: 0 divergences on 78 IPv4 rows.

STILL WORTH SOMETHING: the CURLU-only measurement (strict subset of addr_curl(), never disagreeing where both admit, admitting nothing addr_whatwg() refuses) is a real fact about a layer raddr does not model and rurl does, in R/parse-web.R. That is the boundary RADD-cdmoeadr should be checking when it adds rurl to the migration diff -- not as something raddr should absorb, but as the reason rurl's layer cannot be delegated to addr_curl().

The compose_dialects() note stands on its own: it expresses fallback precedence only, and a URL-host gate is guard-then-parse. Relevant if raddr ever grows a URL-layer dialect. Not v0.1.

Also worth recording somewhere durable: --proxy and --doh-url both remove getaddrinfo from curl's path, and getaddrinfo IS curl's leniency. Any offline curl probe measures a layer that never occurs in a real invocation.

#### 2026-07-29 — 142225707+bart-turczynski@users.noreply.github.com

Closed as SUPERSEDED, 2026-07-29. Not done -- the work it asked for turned out to be already in the tree, and the premise it was filed on had been retracted.

Verified against the repository rather than taken from the 2026-07-28 comment:

- tests/testthat/fixtures/ipv4-oracle.csv has header input,pton,aton,getaddrinfo,whatwg,netip,curl
- tests/testthat/fixtures/ipv6-oracle.csv has header input,pton,aton,getaddrinfo,gai_scope,pyip,pyip_zone,whatwg,netip,netip_zone,curl
- test-ipv4.R asserts addr_curl() against that column across the sweep, and pins 192.0.048.1 -> 192.0.48.1 and 0177.0.0.1 -> 127.0.0.1 by name
- test-ipv6.R:142 'real curl reaches getaddrinfo for IPv6, which settles O13', plus test-ipv6.R:169 pinning the exact ten lift rows the fallback fix moved

Probing CURLU with the resolver removed -- which is what the proposed --proxy oracle would have done -- would have measured the wrong thing and could have 'disproved' a correct implementation. **Status:** done | **Parent:** pbwpleuzfntiksjhkjicnjrgyxkthhqd

#### 2026-07-30 — bartek@turczynski.pl

FILED as RURL-hikovisr in rurl's own local tracker (low, parent RURL-hpiatpfk 'Epic: rurl package active code work'). Same route as the four sitemapr/robotstxtr reports: a sibling repo's local fp tracker needs no network, so the GitHub suspension blocks only a fix PR, not the report. rurl's working tree was not touched.

VERIFIED, not restated. Read-only against ~/Projects/rurl at feat/serialize-url 9625749 (rurl 2.8.0), with every line citation also checked against main (c0c8dca) because both files differ across the two branches.

Mechanism: R/accessors.R:1212 defaults url_standard = NULL; R/diagnostics.R:562 on main (:569 on the branch) short-circuits ._url_metadata_vec() and returns all-NA BEFORE ._parse_stage_a_vec() runs. The gate block is byte-identical on both branches, and both signatures sit at the same lines on each, so the report holds on main. Silent -- no error, warning or message.

FOUR THINGS THIS ISSUE'S TEXT DID NOT HAVE:

1. The real defect is an OVERLOAD, not the NULL default. get_host_type(c('/relative/path',''), url_standard='rfc3986') and get_host_type(c('http://example.com/','http://x.test/')) are identical() -- both c(NA,NA). So a caller who forgets the argument gets output that reads as 'rurl could not classify any of my URLs'. That is the fixable part, and it is fixable WITHOUT a default flip. Filed on that framing rather than 'a default that answers nothing'.

2. It is a family, not one function. Same gate covers get_scheme_class() (R/accessors.R:1488, docs at :1450 explicitly 'mirroring get_host_type()'s contract') and get_url_diagnostics() (character(0) per row). Note which one escapes: get_scheme_class() has a distinct 'missing-or-error' token for failed rows, so it does NOT collide. The two helpers returning a bare NA/character(0) are exactly the two that do.

3. ADR 0007 is not challengeable here, and the report says so. It records 'No default flip... A default change would be a future major.' get_host_type() shipped in 2.2.0 (tag v2.2.0, commit e3d2b65, RURL-csdrxdoj), so the default is published contract. Filed with three non-breaking options (docs / signal a condition / sentinel token) and a recommendation of docs+condition, explicitly leaving the choice to rurl's owner. The condition option has in-package precedent: canonical_join()'s classed legacy-dial warning in 2.8.0.

4. rurl HAD ALREADY FOUND THIS AND CLOSED THE AUDIT WITHOUT TRIAGING IT. RURL-zjbzdmdr (done) lists it as candidate divergence #1, 'Companion helpers silent without url_standard... Bug or doc gap?'. Its AC2 required a follow-up ticket for every BUG verdict and AC3 an ADR entry for every deliberate boundary; the triage that actually ran covered only the WPT slice (bucket A -> RURL-cdjnhnvf, bucket B -> ADR 0004 addendum). Candidates #2 and #3 were later handled; #1 got neither verdict nor ticket. raddr reaching the same finding independently from outside is the useful signal, and RURL-hikovisr now carries it. Left a retro-note on RURL-zjbzdmdr rather than reopening it.

Also checked: this is not a duplicate. RURL-cbrfphfr (the raddr IP-delegation ticket) already NAMED RADD-dumjpoub in its description and scoped it 'small and independent of this migration' -- but it had no issue of its own. Commented there too, pointing at RURL-hikovisr and noting it is unblocked by the raddr release chain. No labels set: rurl registers a labels multiselect but no issue uses it, so none were invented.

Counterpoint recorded in the report, not suppressed: the docs' justification for the gate (R/accessors.R:1196-1199, 'a question only a standard answers, so with no selector there is no fact to report') is sound and matches raddr's own facts-not-verdicts posture. The objection is narrower -- if there is no fact, NA is the wrong way to say so, because NA already means something else. Supporting evidence that the gate was a per-function judgement rather than a blanket rule: get_parse_verdicts() is deliberately ungated and returns real verdicts with no selector (confirmed by running it), and is_valid_host()/check_hosts() both default to url_standard='whatwg'. rurl already ships more than one default on this axis.

## RADD-dwhatxpt: Settle O10: licence mechanics for bundled third-party test data

**Status:** done | **Parent:** vsthdwxndzkdtbikhhcrjosjpqtfzqlg

### Description

Decide how BSD-3 WPT data is carried inside an MIT package under CRAN rules. Blocks RADD-xdgfyznt and RADD-aitbetjb. Measure the LICENSE stub rules rather than reciting them; survey real CRAN-accepted precedent for the file layout.

### Comments

#### 2026-07-28 — 142225707+bart-turczynski@users.noreply.github.com

Evidence gathered before deciding.

MEASURED, not recited — tools:::.license_component_is_for_stub_and_ok is the function R CMD check uses to validate a '+ file LICENSE' stub. For MIT it requires the LICENSE file to parse as DCF with EXACTLY the field set {YEAR, COPYRIGHT HOLDER}. Probed five variants:

  bare two-line template            -> 0 OK
  template + prose paragraph        -> 2 unreadable as DCF
  template + extra DCF field        -> 3 wrong field set
  template + full BSD-3 text        -> 2 unreadable as DCF
  template + ORGANIZATION           -> 3 wrong field set

So every way of putting BSD-3 information into LICENSE breaks the check. LICENSE must stay exactly two lines. A blank line makes DCF start a second record, so appended prose does not merely look wrong, it stops parsing.

PRIOR ART, surveyed live across 266 installed packages: LICENSE.note appears in ZERO of them. inst/COPYRIGHTS appears in 10 (AsioHeaders, callr, diffobj, foreign, fs, pak, processx, remotes, survival, vroom), with 3 more using AUTHORS for the same purpose. fs and vroom are the exact analogue — MIT R packages bundling third-party permissive-licensed material — and both pair the file with a person(role='cph', comment='<what they hold>') entry in Authors@R. O10's original wording ('LICENSE.note handling needs checking') named the wrong instrument.

WPT licence verified at source (raw.githubusercontent.com/web-platform-tests/wpt/master/LICENSE.md): 3-Clause BSD, holder 'web-platform-tests contributors'.

#### 2026-07-28 — 142225707+bart-turczynski@users.noreply.github.com

Settled and committed as 5921562. Written up as docs/architecture.md section 12.1; the section 10 O10 row now carries the verdict.

Resolution in four parts:
1. License: field stays 'MIT + file LICENSE'. LICENSE stays the bare two-line template — measured, there is no alternative that passes.
2. Third-party terms go in inst/COPYRIGHTS, reproduced in full. Not LICENSE.note.
3. Authors@R gains person('web-platform-tests contributors', role='cph', comment='WPT urltestdata.json test corpus').
4. build-registry.R must COMPOSE inst/COPYRIGHTS from its generated IANA provenance section plus a static third-party section read from data-raw/. inst/NOTICE is retired into that file. This is the non-obvious part: the script currently overwrites inst/NOTICE wholesale, so licence text appended there would be silently deleted by the next registry rebuild.

Also recorded: the raddr_extra_*.json split is a licence boundary; BSD-3 clause 3 forbids endorsement phrasing in DESCRIPTION/README; the vendored JSON needs section 7.1's .gitattributes + pre-commit exemption or its sha256 pin is a lie.

Implementation deliberately deferred to RADD-xdgfyznt — a cph entry now would name a copyright holder for material not yet in the package. RADD-xdgfyznt and RADD-aitbetjb are unblocked.

## RADD-ehyllbox: addr_within and addr_within_any

**Status:** done | **Parent:** wysgbyngiykiivctaqnhmghrzlaxophi

### Description

The denylist workhorse. Perf target: 1e6 x 200 blocks within 3x of ipaddress's 1.27 s.

### Comments

#### 2026-07-28 — 142225707+bart-turczynski@users.noreply.github.com

Implemented and committed as 75f6a14. R/within.R, 190 tests in test-within.R.

Perf target met on both families, measured at 1e6 x 200 blocks (architecture 11.1.5, block added to bench/record.R):
  IPv4, 25 distinct lengths: 0.677 s vs ipaddress 0.706 s = 0.96x
  IPv6,  8 distinct lengths: 0.236 s vs ipaddress 0.995 s = 0.24x
Target was 3x; the IPv6 case beats the C++ baseline by 4.2x.

The reason is the algorithm rather than R. prefix_match() walks the block table because the registry asks *which* block contains an address (longest-prefix-match); a denylist only asks whether any does. So addr_within_any() groups blocks by prefix length — every block of the same length reduces its addresses to the same key, and membership is one hash lookup. Pass count is the number of distinct lengths, bounded at 32 for IPv4 and 128 for IPv6 regardless of list size. This also answers part of what RADD-rivkgsza exists to measure: for the 'any' question the sorted/trie comparison is moot, because grouping removes the per-block walk entirely.

Design decisions (architecture 6.3.1):
- A bad block errors instead of returning NA — the one place raddr's decoders do not degrade. A malformed address is data; a malformed block is a silent hole in the denylist. A missing address is still NA, never FALSE.
- Host bits set (192.168.1.1/24) refused, not masked; the error names the masked form.
- Blocks parsed with addr_strict(), not addr_pton(), because pton varies by platform (Apple libc strips leading zeros, glibc rejects). A block must mean one thing everywhere.
- Family decides the space, mismatch is FALSE not an error; v6_4in6 searches the IPv6 space.
- No bitwAnd: 2620:4f:8000::/48 and /1 masks are both pinned by tests.

Cross-checked against CPython ipaddress (1221 addresses x 239 blocks, zero mismatches) and against ipaddress on the full 1e6 of each family (zero disagreements, re-checked by the benchmark on every run).

Gate: 1419 tests pass, lint clean, R CMD check --as-cran 0 errors / 0 warnings / 1 pre-existing NOTE.

**Status:** done | **Parent:** dtdcaphzgdcnwmnlxjaomoeceuiscggd

### Description

ipaddress 1.0.3 accepts an IPv6 zone ID and silently discards it: ip_address('fe80::1%lo0') is fe80::1, ip_address('fe80::1%lo0%en0%wat') is also fe80::1, and no accessor recovers it. Truncating at the first % also accepts rows Apple's inet_pton rejects. [verified 2026-07-27]. Third bug for the same package, alongside O11a and O11b. See docs/architecture.md 3.5.2.

### Comments

#### 2026-07-30 — bartek@turczynski.pl

DRAFT COMPLETE, not submitted. _scratch/outbound-drafts/ipaddress-03-discarded-zone.md. Submission blocked -- suspension re-verified today (day 10).

Core claims confirmed against ipaddress 1.0.3. ip_address('fe80::1%lo0') and ('fe80::1%en0') both give fe80::1; 'fe80::1%lo0%en0%wat' also gives fe80::1; no accessor recovers the zone (grep for zone|scope over the namespace returns character(0)); nothing warns; is.na is FALSE for every form.

Measured against socket.inet_pton(AF_INET6) on Apple libc, this machine: it ACCEPTS fe80::1%lo0, fe80::1%, fe80::1%999 and fe80::1%nonexistent-if, and REJECTS only fe80::1%% and fe80::1%lo0%en0%wat. So the claim survives -- and this issue's own example is one of the two real cases -- but it holds only for multi-% forms, and the draft says exactly that with the full table.

Also checked getaddrinfo, which accepts %lo0, %nonexistent-if AND %999. So 'the resolver validates the interface name' is not a claim available to us either; left out rather than implied. Platform claim scoped explicitly to Apple libc / macOS 25.4.0 arm64, not generalised to glibc or musl -- same discipline as the libc-platform-claims work.

ADDED, because it is the most legible harm and this issue did not state it: the discard makes ip_address('fe80::1%lo0') == ip_address('fe80::1%en0') return TRUE. fe80::/10 is per-interface by construction, so those are different destinations collapsed to one value.

Draft offers three directions (reject with a warning / preserve and expose a zone accessor / warn and drop) rather than prescribing one, because preserving has real design consequences the maintainer owns -- whether fe80::1%lo0 == fe80::1 becomes FALSE, and how a zone interacts with network containment. Noted that validating zone syntax instead of truncating at the first % closes the malformed rows regardless of which direction is taken.

Cross-referenced the CPython zone defect (RADD-vnjcbacv) as evidence that zone handling is a common blind spot rather than an exotic ask -- but only as context, not as an argument about ipaddress.

## RADD-fuarjmzn: compose_dialects() has no slot for a guard-then-parse dialect

**Status:** todo

### Description

Split out of RADD-dtmpmpct on 2026-07-29; that issue's measurement half was already satisfied and it was closed as superseded. This is the half that survives, and it is a v0.2 design question, not v0.1 work.

compose_dialects() expresses ONE relationship: fallback precedence. addr_getaddrinfo() is pton falling back to aton; addr_curl() is aton falling back to addr_getaddrinfo. Every dialect raddr ships today fits that shape.

A URL-parser dialect does not. It is GUARD-THEN-PARSE: failing the guard yields 'not an address' rather than the next parser's answer. The current algebra has no slot for that -- a guard failure and a parse failure are the same event to it, and they are not the same event.

Note that raddr already models two things that are guard-shaped and handles both as ad-hoc steps around the composition rather than as algebra (architecture 3.2):

- getaddrinfo's whitespace gate, modelled as a PRE-step, because the precedence is right and the entry point does something extra in front of it.
- Apple getaddrinfo's link-local scope lift, modelled as a POST-step, for the same reason.

So the algebra has been patched twice already at the composition's edges. A third case is the point at which to ask whether the shape should be first-class instead. Not before -- two ad-hoc steps that each pin cleanly are cheaper than a generalization built for a consumer that does not exist yet.

WHO WOULD EXERCISE IT: rurl is the consumer with the gate shape, and RURL-cbrfphfr carries an owner decision of 2026-07-28 to do no further IP work in rurl until raddr ships. So this cannot be designed against a real consumer until after the raddr release, which is another reason it is not v0.1.

Related: RADD-cdmoeadr's migration diff named sitemapr and robotstxtr, neither of which has the gate shape.

## RADD-gutuomse: O18 — file the two reverse_pointer() bugs on davidchall/ipaddress

**Status:** done | **Parent:** dtdcaphzgdcnwmnlxjaomoeceuiscggd

### Description

Both verified live on 2026-07-30 against ipaddress 1.0.3 (macOS, R 4.6.0). Recorded at docs/architecture.md O18 since 2026-07-28 but never given a tracking issue or a draft, unlike O11a/O11b/O15/O16.

Two defects, two adjacent lines of src/reverse_pointer.cpp, both only in the IPv6 branch:

(a) WRONG SUFFIX. The literal is 'ip.arpa'; RFC 3596 section 2.5 specifies IP6.ARPA, RFC 3152 delegates it, and IANA's .arpa registry lists ip6.arpa and in-addr.arpa but has no ip.arpa entry at all. So every IPv6 name the function has ever returned is unresolvable and one character short. reverse_pointer(ip_address('2001:db8::1')) ends '.1.0.0.2.ip.arpa'.

(b) ACCUMULATION. 'std::ostringstream os;' is declared OUTSIDE the per-element loop and never cleared, so element k carries the nibbles of elements 1..k. Measured label counts for rep('::1', 5): 34, 66, 98, 130, 162 — exactly 32 nibbles added per position. os.str() copies a growing buffer, so cost is quadratic in vector length (architecture 11.1.3).

IPv4 is correct on both counts because its branch uses snprintf and never touches os. A scalar call is correct too, which is why this survived.

WHY IT WENT UNNOTICED, and the most useful thing to tell the maintainer: the test suite ASSERTS the bug. tests/testthat/test-reverse_pointer.R hard-codes the expectation '...8.b.d.0.1.0.0.2.ip.arpa', and every test input plus both @examples are length-1, so the accumulation is invisible. Meanwhile man/reverse_pointer.Rd cites RFC-3596 Section 2.5 — the section that says IP6.ARPA.

Fix is small: add the 6, and move the ostringstream inside the loop (or clear it per iteration).

Duplicate check done 2026-07-30 over the web, which the suspension does not block: 12 issues total (only #101 open), nothing touching reverse_pointer, ip6.arpa or vectorized output; 66 PRs, ZERO open, so no fix is in flight. PR #57 'Pointer used by reverse DNS' is where both defects were introduced — the ostringstream was outside the loop in that diff too.

Deliverable is a FILED report. Draft goes to _scratch/outbound-drafts/ipaddress-05-reverse-pointer.md; posting is blocked on the account suspension.

## RADD-hnczgkcf: Provenance lines carried an impossible curl version

**Status:** done | **Parent:** rzdchzcswdehavskhjvpmqoqxodvmooy

### Description

R/dialects.R documents addr_curl() as 'the whole reason 192.0.048.1 reaches a host under curl that a browser refuses to dial'. Measured against curl 8.20.0: false. curl's URL parser treats 192.0.048.1 as a NAME, so curl never dials 192.0.48.1 for that URL.

Sweep of 35 numeric hosts, CURLU vs addr_whatwg()/addr_curl():
- CURLU admits, WHATWG refuses: NONE. The documented claim shape has no witness.
- CURLU refuses, WHATWG admits: 0x, 1.2.3.4.
- CURLU refuses, addr_curl() admits: 4294967296, 192.0.048.1, 09.1.1.1, 0x100000000
- CURLU admits, addr_curl() refuses: NONE
- Both admit and disagree: NONE (either pairing)

So CURLU is a strict subset of addr_curl(). What addr_curl() actually demonstrates is precedence divergence against addr_getaddrinfo(): 0177.0.0.1 is 127.0.0.1 under curl and 177.0.0.1 under getaddrinfo.

Also fixes the provenance line, which reads 'curl 7.1.0 / libcurl 8.14.1' -- an impossible pairing (curl X.Y.Z ships libcurl X.Y.Z; 7.1.0 is from 2000).

RETRACTION. The premise of this issue was wrong and the fix built on it is reverted (81d90b5).

curl DOES dial 192.0.48.1 for http://192.0.048.1/. Verified with the resolver in the path:

  curl -v http://192.0.048.1/  ->  Trying 192.0.48.1:80
  curl -v http://4294967296/   ->  Trying 0.0.0.0:80
  curl -v http://0Xff/         ->  Trying 0.0.0.255:80
  curl -v http://0177.0.0.1/   ->  Trying 127.0.0.1:80

All four match addr_curl(). The documented sentence is correct as written.

My error: I probed CURLU with --proxy to keep the oracle offline. With a proxy, curl does not resolve -- it hands the host to the proxy -- so %{url.host} shows CURLU's output and nothing else. But curl's host handling is CURLU THEN getaddrinfo, and the leniency lives in the second step: CURLU declines to normalize 192.0.048.1, passes it on as a name, and getaddrinfo reads it as an address via pton. Same class of error f958cfa records in section 11.6 for --doh-url, hit through a different instrument.

The 'CURLU is a strict subset of addr_curl()' measurement is still true about CURLU in isolation, but it is not the operative layer and does not support any claim about what curl reaches.

## RADD-idwarbhp: vec_proxy_equal / vec_proxy_compare with the widening fix

**Status:** done | **Parent:** uyvxinkeheygvtjorxvccceaetjeuasm

### Description

CRITICAL (§5.1.1). R reserves 0x80000000 as NA_integer_, so a raw 32-bit word cannot round-trip through integer comparison. Missingness lives in family; a word reading NA_integer_ means the bit pattern, not absence. Proxies widen to double, mapping that pattern to 2^31. ipaddress 1.0.3 ships this bug: ip_address('0.0.0.128') != itself.

## RADD-iuuruodw: Export the tri-valued positive-reachability fact

**Status:** done

### Description

`embedded_is_global()` (R/embedding.R:378-386) is the two-layer factual accessor ssrfr needs: IANA's `globally_reachable` column where the special-purpose layer answered, `category == "global"` where only the address-space layer did, and NA where neither settled it (today: exactly one block, 192.88.99.0/24). It is internal.

The public docs correctly tell policy consumers not to build a deny-list on `category` (R/classify.R:745-752), which leaves an external consumer with no sanctioned way to get the positive fact. The choices are to copy raddr's internal rule into ssrfr and pin it with snapshot tests, or to export it. Copying re-creates the category semantics the docs warn against, in the one package that must not get it wrong.

Requirement: an exported FACT accessor, not a verdict. Three values, NA never collapsed to FALSE. Named so it cannot be read as allow/deny.

Source: ssrfr landscape field note, gap 1 and implication 10 (ssrfr/_scratch/ssrf-landscape-2026-07-31/field-notes/01-local-raddr-rurl.md:337-345,467-471).

## RADD-ixrigcfm: O7 — read rust-url host.rs ~363-512

**Status:** done | **Parent:** pbwpleuzfntiksjhkjicnjrgyxkthhqd

### Description

The IPv6 half. Only the IPv4 half has been read, and IPv6 is the genuinely new work.

### Comments

#### 2026-07-26 — 142225707+bart-turczynski@users.noreply.github.com

Read rust-url host.rs parse_ipv6addr (lines 364-512 of url/src/host.rs, main). Notes for Epic D:

- WHATWG has **no zone ID at all**: '%' hits the catch-all and is a rejection. Zone is a reality-dialect fact only.
- Hextets are capped at 4 hex digits by construction (end = min(len, start+4)); a 5th hex digit then fails the delimiter match. So '00001::' is a rejection, not a wrap.
- One '::' only (compress_pointer already set at a ':' start is an error), and it may sit at either end.
- A ':' consumed after a hextet must be followed by something, so a trailing single ':' is a rejection.
- len < 2 is rejected outright, so a bare ':' fails before anything else.
- piece_pointer == 8 with input left is a rejection, which is what kills '1:2:3:4:5:6:7:8::'.
- The dotted-quad tail is *stricter than the standalone WHATWG IPv4 parser*: decimal only, no leading zero (Some(0) -> error), each part <= 255, exactly four parts, and piece_pointer <= 6 at entry. It does not reuse parse_ipv4addr and does not accept hex, octal, short forms or a trailing dot.
- Assembly is 'pieces[p] * 0x100 + v' with p advancing after the 2nd and 4th number, then a swap loop that slides the pieces after the compression point to the end.

The consequence for Epic C reuse: RADD-lnxbtfqa cannot simply call the Epic C IPv4 engine for the whatwg tail -- whatwg's IPv6 tail is a separate, stricter grammar than whatwg's IPv4. Whether the reality dialects share their IPv4 tail with inet_aton is an oracle question.




## RADD-izeebldt: Test harvest from the research sweep: LPM regressions, corpus literals, a registry invariant

**Status:** done | **Parent:** vsthdwxndzkdtbikhhcrjosjpqtfzqlg

### Description

Concrete test material the research produced. None of it is currently covered.

A machine-checkable registry invariant (free, over all 51 blocks). RFC 6890 section 2.2.1 states exactly ONE cross-column rule: Destination=False implies Forwardable=False AND Globally Reachable=False. There is NO rule tying Source to anything. This pins the five-independent-columns shape the repo chose.

Longest-prefix-match regressions beyond the one carve-out already cited. Each is wrong under first-match-in-file-order:
- 0.0.0.0 must return 0.0.0.0/32, not 0.0.0.0/8
- 255.255.255.255 must return the /32, not 240.0.0.0/4 (they differ in destination)
- 192.88.99.2 must return the LIVE /32 and not inherit the terminated /24's empty policy row
- 100::1 (discard) vs 100:0:0:1::1 (dummy) are different blocks one hex digit apart
- 5f00::/16 (SRv6 SIDs) nests inside the reserved 4000::/3 -- only LPM returns it correctly, and this becomes live once the address-space registries are vendored (RADD-pekbpche)

Boundary facts never asserted either way:
- 192.0.0.0/29 is .0 through .7 ONLY. 192.0.0.8, .9, .10, .170 and .171 are all OUTSIDE it, each with its own row and different policy. Off-by-one prefix arithmetic silently swaps five protocols' semantics. The /29 is also Forwardable=True inside a Forwardable=False /24 -- a more-specific that WIDENS permissions.
- 2001:db8::/32 is NOT inside 2001::/23. The /23 spans 2001:0000:: to 2001:01ff::.
- 255.255.255.255/32 is the only row that is Source=False and Destination=True; 0.0.0.0/8, 0.0.0.0/32, ::/128, 192.0.0.8/32 and 100:0:0:1::/64 are Source=True and Destination=False. Six rows proving any single 'is this usable' boolean is lossy.

Negative test: 2001:200::/48 is real, allocated, globally routed APNIC space. RFC 5180 section 8 as printed names it; Errata 1752 corrects the benchmarking prefix to 2001:2::/48. Assert we never match the wrong one.

Ten corpus literals with no fixture (from docs/research/delta-c-parsers.md):
fe80::a%25en1 and fe80::1%25lo0 (the RFC 6874 spelling, named in architecture.md but never fixtured, now doubly load-bearing since RFC 9844 obsoleted it); ::1%1]foo.bar baz'\" (NCC/OpenJDK zone-boundary truncation); 0x8.0X8.010.8 (mixed radix within one literal -- legal, base-0 strtoul per part, no rule that parts share a radix); 0129.0.0.1 (CVE-2021-29418: invalid octal digit in the FIRST part); 2002:7f00:1:: (6to4 embedding 127.0.0.1 -- the live Symfony CVE-2026-48736 exploit string); 64:ff9b::a00:1 (NAT64 WKP embedding 10.0.0.1: prefix globally reachable, embedding private, simultaneously); ::ffff:169.254.169.254 (IPv4-mapped link-local, the metadata bypass every surveyed guard misses); 1.2.3.4junk (glibc accepts, musl and Apple reject); 100.100.100.200 (Alibaba metadata inside CGNAT, outside every link-local rule); [::] (the http://0/ class localhost trick).

Note 1.2.3.4x already has a corpus row but the fixture records only Apple, so it cannot show the divergence -- the fixture schema may need a per-libc column before glibc/musl rows are meaningful (see RADD-xrgomyhx, O6).

WHY THIS IS THE OWNER DECISION AND NOT AN AGENT ONE. Every available destination means sending the repository somewhere: iCloud Drive exists on this machine and is the path of least resistance, but copying there hands the contents to a third-party service. That is the owner call.

WHAT TO DO. Copy the newest verified bundle to whatever off-machine destination the owner picks, external volume or cloud. Then re-verify at the destination with git bundle verify, because a bundle that copied badly is worse than no bundle: it looks like a backup.

REFRESH DISCIPLINE, recorded in AGENTS.md: regenerate docs/tracker-snapshot.md before taking any bundle intended to be kept, or the bundle carries a stale copy of the only tracker reasoning in git.

## RADD-khefauzg: No extraction API for an operator-configured NAT64 prefix

**Status:** done

### Description

raddr names NAT64 only from the two fixed prefixes, 64:ff9b::/96 and 64:ff9b:1::/48. A network-specific RFC 6052 prefix is invisible to a prefix table, and raddr deliberately says so rather than guessing (R/classify.R:531-534, 590-593; tests/testthat/test-classify.R:602-610). That is the right default and should not change.

What is missing is the opt-in: a caller who KNOWS their operator prefix has no way to ask raddr to read the address under it. The geometry is already public and complete — addr_transition_registry("embeddings") carries all six RFC 6052 lengths, including the two-segment 40/48/56 cases that straddle the u-byte. So the alternative is that every consumer re-implements the segment splice against our own published table, which is the specific mistake the u-byte carve-out exists to prevent.

Shape to decide: something taking (address, prefix, prefix_len), returning an embedding with the extraction marked as caller-asserted rather than prefix-derived. It must not silently widen addr_classify() — an address is still not self-describing, and the result must stay distinguishable from an affirmative match on a fixed prefix.

Scope note: this is a new input channel (external configuration), not a range-table update. Decide it before the API freeze.

Source: ssrfr landscape field note, gap 2 and implication 10 (ssrfr/_scratch/ssrf-landscape-2026-07-31/field-notes/01-local-raddr-rurl.md:304-313,467-471).

### Comments

#### 2026-07-31 — bartek@turczynski.pl

Done in 0494b03 (branch feature/ssrfr-api-seams, local -- push still 403s on the suspension).

addr_nat64_embeddings(x, prefix) returns a list_of<raddr_embedding> shaped exactly as addr_embeddings(): one row per address under the prefix, zero for each that is not. Consumers can treat the two uniformly.

Two deviations from the issue's proposed shape, both deliberate:

- Signature is (x, prefix) with a CIDR string, not (address, prefix, prefix_len). A CIDR cannot disagree with itself, and it matches addr_within(). One prefix per call: two prefixes of different lengths are two readings of the same address, so raddr does not merge them.
- The caller-asserted marker needed a second vocabulary, not a new level. raddr_embedded_kinds means 'what classification can conclude' and an invariant test iterates it; appending nat64_nsp would have broken that and falsified the vocabulary. So raddr_embedding_kinds = raddr_embedded_kinds + nat64_nsp, and the embedding record uses the wider one while addr_embedded_kind() keeps the narrower. nat64_nsp can therefore never appear in a classification, which is the guarantee the issue asked for, stated rather than assumed.

Checked at the source per the issue's implicit ask: RFC 6052 section 3.1's MUST-drop binds the Well-Known Prefix ALONE, and RFC 8215 section 5 says it does not reach the local-use prefix. There is no equivalent requirement for an NSP, so no code is emitted even when the embedded address is non-global. Pair it with addr_global_reachability() (RADD-iuuruodw) for the fact.

Verified against RFC 6052 section 2.4's own table at all six lengths, driven by the prefix strings -- the pre-existing geometry test covers the same table but is handed a prefix length and never sees a prefix, so the parse/derive/match path was untested until now.

One check is on the prefix rather than the address: at /96, and only there, the reserved u-byte falls inside the prefix, so section 2.2's MUST-be-zero is about the caller's configuration and is refused. See RADD-vpoupbus for the address-side gap that turned up while doing this.

## RADD-kurxtbqc: addr_pton()/addr_strict() accept a trailing newline and return a different address

**Status:** done | **Parent:** pbwpleuzfntiksjhkjicnjrgyxkthhqd

### Description

Found while benchmarking O4 (RADD-sbnlhllz).

`addr_pton("1:2:3:4:5:6:7:8\n")` returns `1:2:3:4:5:6:8000:0`. Not NA -- a
parsed address, different from the one the literal names, with **no reason
codes**. Same for addr_strict() and addr_whatwg(). `::1\n` -> `::8000:0`,
`fe80::1\n` -> `fe80::8000:0`, `\n::1` -> `8000::1`.

Two independent defects stacked:

1. **ipv6.R#230 is the only $-anchored pattern in the package under
   `perl = TRUE`.** PCRE lets `$` match before a trailing newline; TRE does
   not. So the hextet validator accepts `"8\n"`. Every other perl site in R/
   uses an unanchored negated class, which is why only IPv6 is affected and
   why the IPv4 path (ipv4.R#80) correctly rejects `1.2.3.4\n`.

2. **The `strtoi()` result is never checked.** The code relies on the
   invariant "if `bad` is FALSE then `strtoi()` succeeded", and nothing
   enforces it. `strtoi("8\n", 16L)` is NA, the `if (any(bad))` zeroing
   branch never runs, and the NA_integer_ bit pattern is then read back as
   the unsigned word 0x80000000 -- which is where every wrong answer above
   gets its `8000` from.

Defect 2 is the deeper one: it converted a validator miss into a silently
wrong address instead of a rejection. Fix both -- `\z` for the anchor, and a
guard so an NA out of `strtoi()` can never be read as an address.

### Comments

#### 2026-07-29 — 142225707+bart-turczynski@users.noreply.github.com

Fixed in d207e88.

Both faults addressed:

1. `ipv6.R` hextet pattern anchored with `\z` instead of `$`. Restores TRE's meaning exactly on all seven anchored patterns tested, and measures fractionally faster than `$` (0.192 s vs 0.203 s on 4e6 pieces).
2. `if (anyNA(value)) bad <- bad | is.na(value)` after the `strtoi()`, reconciling the conversion with the validator. `anyNA()` short-circuits, so the common case pays one scan and no allocation.

All eight probe literals now reject with reason code `bad_hextet` (`bad_embedded_ipv4` for the 4-in-6 one).

Verification:
- Answers diffed against the pre-change code over a 651-row adversarial corpus across addr_parse/strict/whatwg/aton/pton/curl + codes + ends_in_a_number. The trailing-newline rows are the **only** ones that moved.
- Full testthat suite green, all 22 files, including the WPT corpus and the libc fixtures.
- Verify gate: 0 errors, 0 warnings, 1 pre-existing NOTE.

Four regression tests added to `test-ipv6.R` covering the rejection, the reason code, the 0x80000000 signature specifically, and the leading-zero dialect (whose pattern carries the same anchor and still has to admit `00001:2:3:4:5:6:7:8`).

36x on the address-space table addr_classify() reads on every call.

Tie-break checked rather than assumed: order(decreasing = TRUE) was stable so the walk resolved same-length same-key blocks to the earlier row, and split() keeps each group ascending so the groups do too. A test doubles the transition table and pins it.

within.R's within_keys() and the new prefix_keys() were the same three lines, so within.R now calls classify.R's. keys_in_targets() stays as it is -- containment wants the logical.

The new test's oracle is NOT the old walk: it is an independent matcher deciding containment by string prefix (startsWith over addr_to_binary), sharing nothing with prefix_match() but the encoder. Runs over the first and last address of all 340 blocks of all four tables.

Base R trap found writing it: substr(x, 1L, len) truncates len to length(x), so a length-1 address against a vector of prefix lengths silently uses only the first one. Worth remembering.

Suite 1419 -> 1430, lint clean, R CMD check --as-cran 0/0/0.




## RADD-lfgkjvfv: pslr-ize provenance: content-pinned snapshots and an editorial version stamp

**Status:** done | **Parent:** pbwpleuzfntiksjhkjicnjrgyxkthhqd

### Description

Adopt pslr's provenance discipline for the vendored IANA registries.

Today the version stamp is the HTTP Last-Modified of the served CSVs. Verified 2026-07-27, that is a site DEPLOY timestamp, not an editorial one: seven CSV exports across four unrelated IANA registries carry the identical second 'Thu, 09 Oct 2025 21:51:16 GMT', and the IPv4 multicast registry's page records Last Updated 2026-06-26 while several of its own CSV exports still serve a 2025 Last-Modified. The number raddr ships (2025-10-09) happens to be correct, because both special-purpose registries were genuinely edited that day -- right by coincidence. Docs were narrowed to claim only 'when the file was served' rather than 'when IANA last changed it'.

What pslr does that raddr does not: data-raw/update_psl.R pins a 40-char upstream commit SHA and derives list_date from that commit's committer date, so the snapshot is content-addressed and the date is deterministic given the pin. IANA publishes no commit or version to pin, so the analogue has two halves.

1. Stamp from the page-level 'Last Updated' field inside the registry XHTML -- IANA's own editorial date -- instead of the HTTP header. Cost: build-registry.R must fetch the XHTML as well as the CSV, and scrape a field. The failure mode is SAFE: an unparseable field yields NA, and NA already yields addr_registry_outdated() == TRUE. So this is a cost decision, not a risk one.

2. Consider making the snapshot content-addressed the way pslr's is. sha256 per file is already recorded and --check already compares content and never dates, so most of this exists; what is missing is a single snapshot identity a user can quote.

Deferred deliberately in favour of a light-touch doc correction (see architecture.md section 7.1). Revisit if a second registry is vendored, since the IANA address-space registries DO carry divergent editorial dates and the header approach would misdate them by up to eight months.

Evidence: docs/research/01-iana-registries.md (Source metadata table, gotcha 33) and docs/research/delta-a-registries.md A1.

--check gained two independent snapshot steps and stays dates-blind: manifest-vs-disk catches content drift, id-vs-its-own-manifest catches a hand-edited sysdata.rda that nothing else would see. digest added to Suggests so the test suite recomputes the id rather than trusting it, with a mutation test proving the assertion can fail (one flipped hex digit, and a reordered manifest, both move the id).

## RADD-mnzchljx: Edge-case vignette, generated from exported accessors rather than hand-maintained

**Status:** done | **Parent:** rzdchzcswdehavskhjvpmqoqxodvmooy

### Description

A user-facing 'be warned' catalogue, distinct from docs/architecture.md (decisions, for contributors) and docs/research/ (raw evidence, for us). Ships as vignette('edge-cases').

DEFERRED deliberately (2026-07-27): too early to generate auto-docs. Revisit once Epics I-K have landed and there is enough to put in it.

The design constraint that matters: GENERATE the tables, do not hand-maintain them. A stale warnings document is worse than none, because people trust it. Most content is already queryable from exported accessors and can be rendered at vignette build time:

- reason codes and spec violations -> addr_codes_registry() (code, layer, strength, rfc, summary, since). Cannot drift; it IS the vocabulary the engines emit.
- the divergence matrix -> tests/testthat/fixtures/ipv4-oracle.csv (91 inputs) and ipv6-oracle.csv (126 inputs). These are live measurements against real libc, Python and ada, so the published warnings are literally the measurements, and re-running the oracle scripts updates the document.
- registry facts -> addr_registry(): the two N/A rows, the two termination dates, the carve-outs that force longest-prefix match.
- provenance -> addr_registry_version(), addr_transition_version(), and the deploy-timestamp caveat (RADD-lfgkjvfv).

Roughly 20% is irreducibly hand-written framing and should stay short: why glibc and musl disagree on '1.2.3.4junk', why WHATWG contradicts itself on leading zeros between a standalone host and an IPv6 dotted tail, why RFC 6890's tables must not be trusted as data.

Dependency note to decide explicitly when this lands: a vignette pulls knitr and rmarkdown into Suggests. No runtime dependency, but it is the first crack in 'vctrs + rlang, argue about anything else' (architecture.md section 12), so it should be an argued addition rather than a silent one.

Source material: docs/research/*.md and the three delta files.

### Comments

#### 2026-07-29 — 142225707+bart-turczynski@users.noreply.github.com

Done in d1cb086 on feature/wpt-corpus (local; push still blocked). Ships as vignette('edge-cases').

Held the design constraint: GENERATED, not hand-maintained. Every table is computed at build time from the six dialect functions, addr_registry(), addr_codes_registry() and the four version accessors.

One deviation from the ticket's plan, and it is a robustness fix rather than a shortcut. The ticket proposed sourcing the divergence matrix from tests/testthat/fixtures/ipv4-oracle.csv and ipv6-oracle.csv. A shipped vignette cannot reliably read those: docs/ and data-raw/ are .Rbuildignore'd, and reaching into ../tests/ from vignettes/ works today only because tests/ happens to be in the tarball -- one .Rbuildignore edit away from silently breaking. So the matrix is computed by calling raddr's own dialects over curated inputs. The oracle CSVs still do their job one layer down: test-ipv4.R and test-ipv6.R assert raddr against them, so the vignette's numbers are the measured ones by transitivity, and re-running the oracle scripts still propagates. Only the CHOICE of which rows to show is editorial; every answer is computed.

TWO CHUNKS WERE WRONG IN THE FIRST DRAFT and both would have shipped looking authoritative. Worth recording because 'generated' is not the same as 'correct':

1. The longest-prefix-match carve-outs were selected with prefix_len > 8 -- a proxy for nesting, not nesting. It also computed a 'parents' set and never used it. That listed 14 blocks, of which 5 (192.31.196.0/24, 192.52.193.0/24, 192.175.48.0/24, 64:ff9b::/96, 2620:4f:8000::/48) are globally reachable but NOT inside a non-globally-reachable parent, so they are not carve-outs at all. Replaced with real containment: each block's network address through addr_within_any() against every block IANA marks not globally reachable. Nine genuine carve-outs. Found by re-reading the knitted output, not the source.
2. The zone section asserted the %25lo0 form without showing what raddr does with it. raddr reads a zone as literal text and does NOT percent-decode, so %25lo0 gives zone '25lo0', not 'lo0'. Correct behaviour -- decoding is a URL-layer step and raddr never sees a URL -- but a trap in its own right, so it is now shown rather than implied.

Content: the leading zero and 192.0.048.1; short forms and the unchecked whole-host number; the WHATWG asymmetry (a leading zero is a warning in a standalone host, a hard failure in an IPv6 dotted tail, because the tail is a separate stricter loop); IPv6 hextet width; the zone; the three-way Apple/glibc/musl split on trailing garbage with raddr shipping one of three; LPM carve-outs; 0.0.0.0/8 vs 0.0.0.0/32 which RFC 6890 Table 2 collapsed; the twelve forwardable-but-not-globally-reachable blocks; the four N/A rows and the two distinct reasons behind one NA; RFC 6890 as a thirteen-year-stale snapshot; provenance stamps and addr_registry_outdated().

Added from the research deltas: RFC 9844 (Aug 2025) completely obsoletes RFC 6874, so zone-in-URI has no live standard.

DEPENDENCY NOTE, which the ticket asked to be decided explicitly: no argument needed. knitr and rmarkdown were already in Suggests before this vignette, and the owner's position is that the vctrs + rlang budget governs the CORE LOGIC, not the tooling that documents the package. Docs are wanted, so the tooling that produces them is suggested.

Verified: lintr clean; R CMD check --as-cran 0 errors, 0 warnings, 1 pre-existing NOTE; all three vignettes re-build OK under a real install.

Steps 1-5 of the handover agenda, all by hand-evaluation rather than by re-running the suite.

**1. slow_v6() elision arithmetic vs RFC 4291 s2.2 — clean.** Built the piece count and quad position for all eleven listed forms from the RFC first, then read the code. The two sides turn out to implement the same predicate written twice: shipped 'ifelse(elided, gap >= 1L, gap == 0L)' over 'gap = 8 - pieces(head) - pieces(tail)' with the quad already stood down to the placeholder '0:0'; naive 'if (elided) given >= 8L else given != 8L' with 'length(quad) == 2'. ## RADD-mvtkwncu: O17 — why the raddr_parse record costs 2x more to build for IPv6 than IPv4

**Status:** done | **Parent:** pbwpleuzfntiksjhkjicnjrgyxkthhqd

### Description

Measured 2026-07-27, architecture 11.1.1: the record (outcomes, codes, derived status) costs 2.5 s per 1e6 on IPv4 and 5.7 s on IPv6, on top of four engines that are at or below the 4x floor. The flat-per-row theory does not explain it.

Unverified suspicion: derive_status() -> readings_agree(). For an IPv6 vector, aton's reading is missing on every row, so vec_equal() against an all-missing address enters addr_proxy_equal()'s blank_missing(), which does proxy[is.na(code), ] <- NA over 1e6 rows and 6 columns. An all-accepted IPv4 vector never takes that path.

If that is the cause, the fix is to skip dialects that accepted nothing in readings_agree(), and to avoid computing vec_equal() on rows where accepts is FALSE. Small. Profile first -- do not optimize on the strength of the guess.

Not a blocker: addr_parse() has no stated performance target and the reason codes measured close to free (under 0.1x).

### Comments

#### 2026-07-29 — 142225707+bart-turczynski@users.noreply.github.com

Profiled 2026-07-29, commit 41c36d5. The hypothesis is falsified, and so is the question's premise.

THE RECORD DOES NOT COST MORE FOR IPv6. derive_status() is 0.124 s on IPv4 against 0.116 s on IPv6 at the same vector length. Flat. The whole record layer -- derive_status, readings_agree, first_code, outcome_factor, new_raddr_parse -- is 8% of the call on IPv4 and 2% on IPv6.

THE SPECIFIC SUSPICION WAS RIGHT ABOUT THE PATH AND WRONG ABOUT THE COST. blank_missing()'s proxy[is.na(code), ] <- NA over the all-missing aton column IS taken on every IPv6 row, exactly as described. It costs 0.030 s of 9.138 s -- 0.4% of the call. The proposed fix (skip dialects that accepted nothing) would not pay for its own branch.

WHERE 2.5 s / 5.7 s CAME FROM. Subtraction: addr_parse() minus the bare dialect functions. That charges the record for parse_dialect_full(), which is 71% (v4) / 76% (v6) of the call. addr_parse() cannot use the bare dialects -- it needs to know whether each dialect ATTEMPTED an input to tell malformed from not_an_address -- and ip_attempt()/ends_in_a_number() are ~22% of the call in BOTH families. Per dialect, not per row, which is exactly why the flat-per-row theory could not predict it. Architecture 11.1.1's '+ the record' row is mislabelled and now says so.

Rprof, 3 runs of 3e5, addr_parse total 9.138 s (v6) / 4.926 s (v4):
  parse_dialect_full   6.960 (76.17%) | 3.490 (70.82%)
  parse_ipv6_addr      5.080 (55.59%) | --
  ip_attempt           1.972 (21.58%) | 1.176 (23.86%)
  parse_ipv4_addr      1.676 (18.34%) | 3.352 (68.02%)
  derive_status        0.116 ( 1.27%) | 0.124 ( 2.52%)
  blank_missing        0.030 ( 0.33%) | 0.002 ( 0.06%)

ONE REAL TARGET, filed separately as RADD-tkpqvomv rather than taken here: parse_ipv4_number_slow() is 13% of an IPv6 parse. Every IPv6 literal is a single non-decimal part to the IPv4 engines, so it declines parse_ipv4_number()'s fast path and does hex/octal/width/truncation work before the alphabet walk finds the ':' and rejects. A union-alphabet pre-filter would likely take most of it, but it is the hottest correctness path in the package and wants its own change with its own evidence.

No code change here, per the issue's own instruction.

## RADD-nfmidnil: Longest-prefix-match lookup

**Status:** done | **Parent:** vbsszjhsnayjncvmiuelqdfxftibjwri

### Description

Flat first-match-wins does not work: 192.0.0.9/32 and 192.0.0.10/32 are globally reachable inside a non-global 192.0.0.0/24.

### Comments

#### 2026-07-27 — 142225707+bart-turczynski@users.noreply.github.com

Done in c7b0ea6. Internal registry_match(): index sorted by descending prefix length, first hit wins. Verified against the 192.0.0.0/24 carve-outs, 0.0.0.0/32-in-/8, and 2001::/32-in-/23.

Two findings worth carrying forward:

1. The matcher uses NO bitwise operation. Words are raw bit patterns with NA_integer_ meaning 0x80000000 (§5.1.1), and R's bit operators break on that in both directions, silently: bitwAnd of the pattern reads as missing, and bitwNot(2147483647) is itself NA so a /1 mask cannot be spelled. The first is live -- 2620:4f:8000::/48 holds 0x80000000 in w2, so a bitwise matcher never matches the AS112 direct-delegation prefix and fails as a miss rather than an error. Containment is integer division over widen_word()'s unsigned double proxy. This is §12's arithmetic constraint in a THIRD form (shift, operand, and now mask-and-operand both).

2. v6_4in6 searches the IPv6 half only: ::ffff:127.0.0.1 matches ::ffff:0:0/96, never 127.0.0.0/8. Collapsing those would destroy the scope/embedded_scope distinction before Epic I even builds it.

42 tests, incl. every block's own network address round-tripped through the matcher. Lint clean, full suite 513 passing.
