## RADD-pekbpche: Vendor the two IANA address-space registries as a fallback layer

**Status:** done | **Parent:** vbsszjhsnayjncvmiuelqdfxftibjwri

### Description

Extend data-raw/build-registry.R to vendor the IANA IPv4 Address Space registry (256 /8 rows) and the IPv6 Address Space registry (20 rows), with the same sha256 + --check discipline as the special-purpose pair. Do NOT vendor the IPv6 Global Unicast Assignments registry: it is not a partition (61 sub-ranges of 2000::/3 appear in no row), so absence there means 'unallocated', a different answer from 'not found'.

Why: both address-space registries are exact partitions of their spaces, so classification becomes TOTAL and 'global' becomes a statement backed by a registry row instead of an absence. Deriving a table from the special-purpose registry alone is a known CVE-producing pattern -- multicast is not in that registry, which is why PHP's registry-derived rewrite has no multicast handling and ssrfcheck shipped CVE-2025-8267. See architecture.md P9.

Layering: IANA states the precedence itself. The address-space registries carry 'For authoritative registration, see [Special-Purpose Address Space]', so Special-Purpose outranks Address Space by the source's own instruction. Confirmed overlaps: fc00::/7, fe80::/10, ff00::/8, 2001::/23, 2002::/16, 3fff::/20, 240.0.0.0/4 and eleven IPv4 blocks.

The five policy columns do not exist in the address-space registries, so a match there yields scope + name + rfc with all five policy logicals NA -- the same treatment previously proposed for unmatched addresses. The special-purpose registry answers policy; the address-space registry answers identity; neither invents the other's answer.

Known parsing traps, all already documented in docs/research/01-iana-registries.md:
- the IPv4 Prefix column is '000/8'...'255/8', NOT CIDR
- the IPv4 CSV header literally reads 'Status [1]', so matching on 'Status' fails
- IPv6 spells prefixes compressed: ::/8, 100::/8, 200::/7, e000::/4, fe00::/9 -- not 0000::/8
- ipv6-address-space.csv 404s and serves a 4216-byte HTML error body; the real file is ipv6-address-space-1.csv
- the CSV export corrupts the RDAP column (two URLs concatenated without a separator) on every ARIN/AFRINIC row -- not a column raddr needs, but do not assume CSV fidelity per-column
- footnote [14] sources multicast as RFC 5771; footnote [17] sources 240/4 as RFC 1112

Also update section 7's '4712 bytes, 51 blocks' framing, and give inst/extdata the finding-4 hook exemption for any new vendored CSV.

Provenance caveat: these two registries carry editorial dates that differ from their served Last-Modified, unlike the special-purpose pair. See RADD-lfgkjvfv.

### Comments

#### 2026-07-27 — 142225707+bart-turczynski@users.noreply.github.com

Done, b00a5b5. Both registries vendored with the same sha256 + --check discipline; 276 rows (256 v4, 20 v6) in a SEPARATE sysdata table with addr_address_space() and addr_address_space_version(). Both partitions asserted at build time.

Four things the build measured that this issue got wrong or did not know:

1. The predicted overlap ('fc00::/7, fe80::/10, ff00::/8, 2001::/23, 2002::/16, 3fff::/20, 240.0.0.0/4 and eleven IPv4 blocks') does not survive measurement. Since the address-space pair is an exact partition, EVERY special-purpose block is contained in one of its rows, so containment is not a meaningful count. Exact-prefix equality is: five, namely 0.0.0.0/8, 10.0.0.0/8, 127.0.0.0/8, fc00::/7, fe80::/10.

2. 8000::/3 stores w1 as 0x80000000 -- R's NA_integer_ pattern. Section 5.1.1 was already load-bearing for 2620:4f:8000::/48, but that was a /48; this is an eighth of the IPv6 address space, and a naive numeric read makes the partition check silently mis-tile rather than fail.

3. The four vendored files are NOT served with one Last-Modified. Three carry Thu 09 Oct 2025 21:51:16 GMT, the IPv6 address-space export carries Sat 11 Oct 2025 00:06:16 GMT. So the 'older of the two halves' rule, which section 7.1 records as a no-op for the special-purpose pair, actually bites for this one. Stamped separately (space_version), per section 7.2's principle.

4. The 'finding-4 hook exemption' was already in place: .gitattributes has inst/extdata/*.csv -text and pre-commit excludes ^inst/extdata/, both by path prefix, so the new CSVs inherited it. Nothing to add.

Every documented parsing trap reproduced exactly: 000/8 not CIDR, 'Status [1]' header, ipv6-address-space.csv 404ing into a 4216-byte HTML body, RDAP concatenating two URLs on every ARIN/AFRINIC row. WHOIS and RDAP are dropped from the parsed table (corrupt, and not raddr's question); the vendored bytes keep them.

## RADD-purmngor: Revisit: should addr_codes_registry() carry the per-code documentation fields, once ssrfr work starts

**Status:** todo

### Description

Deferred from RADD-kdpoamxh, 2026-07-29. NOT v0.1 work — deliberately parented at top level rather than under the v0.1 root.

RADD-kdpoamxh asked for four things per code: meaning, why it is a signal, detection and precision, and an example. The registry (R/codes.R, exported as addr_codes_registry()) carries only the first, as 'summary', alongside code/layer/rfc/strength/since. Three shapes were considered; a prose vignette won for v0.1 because 'why it is a signal' and 'precision' — what a code does NOT prove — need room that a data frame cell does not give them.

THE OPTION HELD OPEN HERE is the second shape: add the fields to the registry as columns, making them machine-readable so ssrfr can consume them rather than restating them.

Why it was deferred and not rejected:

- Architecture 5.2.2 makes the registry an API surface. Adding a code is an API addition; adding a COLUMN that another package pins against is a larger commitment in the same direction, and it should be made when there is a real consumer with real requirements, not speculatively.
- The consumer relationship is narrower than raddr's docs used to claim. ssrfr ADR-001 section 7 assigns the reason-code vocabulary and result model to ssrfr; its spec 5.2 fixes its codes as kebab-case, normative for ssrfr and constrained by ITS OWN published consumers, with the case divergence called deliberate. The relationship is many-to-one and conditional: raddr states facts, ssrfr interprets them into a refusal reason, and a raddr code may travel in a detailed ssrfr result as evidence without being its public reason.
- So the question this issue actually asks is: does ssrfr want structured evidence fields from raddr, or only the codes themselves? That is answerable by ssrfr, not by raddr, and it is cheap to add columns later and expensive to remove them.

WHEN TO PICK THIS UP: at the start of ssrfr work, with ssrfr's evidence model in hand.

Note in passing: man/addr_codes_registry.Rd carried the retracted claim that 'ssrfr reports raddr's codes rather than inventing a parallel vocabulary'. That is a separate defect and is being fixed under RADD-kdpoamxh; it is not what this issue is about.



## RADD-puzhycev: addr_curl() composes the wrong fallback for IPv6: getaddrinfo, not pton

**Status:** done | **Parent:** vsthdwxndzkdtbikhhcrjosjpqtfzqlg

### Description

Measured against real curl 8.20.0 by the RADD-xpmuxafb oracle. addr_curl() is compose_dialects(addr_aton(x), addr_pton(x)). Real curl composes aton then getaddrinfo. For IPv4 the two are indistinguishable (0 divergences on 78 measurable rows) because getaddrinfo reduces to pton once aton has rejected. For IPv6 aton rejects everything, so the composition IS the fallback, and pton and getaddrinfo disagree wherever Apple's getaddrinfo lifts an embedded scope out of a link-local address (section 3.5.3). 10 of 88 measurable rows are wrong.

Candidate fix is one line: compose_dialects(addr_aton(x), addr_getaddrinfo(x)). Measured to give 0 divergences in BOTH families.

Ripples: section 3.2, the curl column of section 3.3's table (derived, never measured), the Compositions section of R/dialects.R roxygen, and the pinned-defect test in test-ipv6.R which is written to fail when the fix lands.

### Comments

#### 2026-07-28 — 142225707+bart-turczynski@users.noreply.github.com

Fixed in 99c7253. addr_curl() = compose_dialects(addr_aton(x), addr_getaddrinfo(x)).

Swapped in all three implementations of the composition: R/dialects.R, composed_reading() in R/parse.R, and slow_parse_one() in helper-slow.R. Full suite green, lintr clean, R CMD check --as-cran 0 errors / 0 warnings / 1 pre-existing NOTE (unpublished repo URL).

Two things the fix turned up that were not in the ticket:

1. The getaddrinfo whitespace gate is inherited but UNOBSERVABLE through curl. The gate tests the text before the '%', which is exactly the address text, and pton refuses whitespace there anyway -- so wherever the gate would bite, aton has already answered. That means addr_curl() needs no gate of its own. Pinned by running compose(aton, ungated-gai) against addr_curl() over the whole corpus, not left as prose.

2. The outcome and code surfaces (composition_parts, addr_outcome, addr_codes) correctly keep naming the two PRIMITIVES rather than following the reading's fallback. getaddrinfo accepts what pton accepts plus what aton accepts, and aton has already run; the scope lift moves bits, never acceptance. So curl's acceptance set is still aton union pton. New test in test-parse.R pins that, so the mismatch between the reading path and the outcome path cannot read as stale.

Ripples landed: section 3.2 (both the code block and a new paragraph on why the fallback is the entry point rather than the parser under it), section 3.5's table + the aton bullet in 3.5.1, section 11.6, the O13 row, the dialects roxygen + man/dialects.Rd, and both README tables. The pinned-defect test in test-ipv6.R is gone; its ten named rows survive as the set where addr_curl() and addr_pton() now part company -- the same set from the other side.

Section 3.5's curl column is now a copy of the getaddrinfo one. Left in place with a line saying that is the finding (aton rejects every IPv6 literal, so the composition is nothing but its fallback), rather than dropped as redundant.

## RADD-rivkgsza: Benchmark trie vs sorted masked vector

**Status:** done | **Parent:** vbsszjhsnayjncvmiuelqdfxftibjwri

### Description

O5. Benchmark the longest-prefix-match lookup: trie vs sorted masked vector vs the current linear scan over blocks sorted by descending prefix length. Table size is 51 IANA blocks (NOT 53 -- that was a line count; see architecture.md section 7.1) plus the 8-row transition overlay, plus roughly 18 IANA address-space rows if the multicast/reserved addition lands. Probably neither a trie nor triebeard at this size, but measure. Use bench/record.R's best-of-seven: a ratio divided by a sub-second baseline needs it, and a single system.time() already put one wrong number into the design record (corrected in 55b4605). Run on an idle machine.

### Comments

#### 2026-07-28 — 142225707+bart-turczynski@users.noreply.github.com

Partial answer from RADD-ehyllbox (commit 75f6a14), which had to solve the neighbouring problem.

For the 'does any block contain this address' question, neither a trie nor a sorted masked vector is needed: grouping the blocks by prefix length removes the per-block walk entirely. Every block of the same length reduces its addresses to the same key (the top len bits), so membership is one hash lookup per distinct length. Pass count is bounded at 32 for IPv4 and 128 for IPv6 regardless of how many blocks there are. Measured 1e6 x 200 blocks: IPv4 0.677 s (0.96x of ipaddress), IPv6 0.236 s (0.24x).

That does NOT settle this issue, because the registry asks a different question — *which* block matches, longest-prefix-match — and grouping by length does not order the answers. prefix_match()'s descending-length walk is still the thing to benchmark, over 51 registry blocks. But it does mean the comparison should be scoped to the longest-prefix-match case rather than to containment generally, and R/within.R is a worked example of what the flat walk costs when the ordering is not needed.

#### 2026-07-28 — 142225707+bart-turczynski@users.noreply.github.com

bench/prefix.R (25188dc) measures four candidates at 1e6 addresses over the special and space tables. Answer: none of the three O5 named.

The regrouping RADD-ehyllbox built for containment answers longest-prefix-match too. vec_match() returns the position where vec_in() returns a logical, so a length group reports *which* block matched; visiting groups longest-first keeps first-hit-wins, because anything matched later is shorter by construction.

Grouped wins every case:
  special v4 random  0.280 -> 0.175 s (0.63x)
  special v6 random  0.309 -> 0.211 s (0.68x)
  special v4 inside  0.352 -> 0.156 s (0.44x)
  special v6 inside  0.409 -> 0.216 s (0.53x)
  space   v4 random  1.637 -> 0.031 s (0.019x)  <- 53x
  space   v6 random  0.810 -> 0.152 s (0.19x)

The space row is the finding: 276 rows collapse to 9 groups because its 256 IPv4 rows are all /8, and addr_classify() reads that table on every call.

Sorted masked vector is 1.6-3.0x SLOWER than the walk on special -- a binary search is log2(m) passes where a hash is one, and vectorized in R each pass costs an n-sized ifelse(). The trie cannot read the words at all: triebeard wants character keys, so every call re-encodes 1e6 addresses into bit strings, 128 chars each for IPv6.

Gated on agreement: all four vs the shipped prefix_match() over 6e6 random rows plus the first and last address of every block in all four tables. 30 counts, all 0. Recorded as section 11.1.6.

Framed as "does base R suffice" rather than "which is faster", because stringi is 34.7 MB, is C++ bundling ICU, and declares `SystemRequirements: ICU4C` — against a package whose DESCRIPTION says it is pure R. And the strong case for stringi (locale-independent Unicode, which is why rurl pays for it) is **absent**: `R/encoding.R` gates the input and the hextet/octet grammars are ASCII by definition. So only speed could carry it.

Base R is three engines, not one, so every pattern ran under TRE, PCRE and ICU with agreement asserted:

| pattern | TRE | PCRE | ICU |
|---|---|---|---|
| ipv6#210 `(^:|::|:$)` | 0.517 | **0.319** | 0.373 |
| ipv6#230 hextet | 1.030 | **0.422** | 0.554 |
| ipv4#245 `^0[0-9]` | 0.163 | **0.071** | 0.223 |
| ipv6#137 `sub(^.*:)` | 0.751 | **0.310** | 0.387 |
| strsplit flat v6 | **0.561** | — | 0.729 |
| strtoi base 16 | **0.214** | — | *no analogue* |

**PCRE ahead of ICU on all ten patterns.** Splits a wash; stringi's `simplify = NA` matrix — the one structural rather than constant-factor advantage available — is *slower* than `unlist(strsplit())`. stringi wins nchar/strrep/paste0, all sub-0.1 s stages. Its one real win is `stri_detect_charclass()` (0.169 vs 0.386 for today's anchored regex), and restructuring in base R as a negated scan + `nchar()` reaches 0.260 — two-thirds of it, free. Tagging input UTF-8 moves neither engine, so the gap is engine speed, not marshalling.

**What it actually yielded was a bug.** Asking what `perl = TRUE` changes besides speed: PCRE's `$` matches before a trailing newline, TRE's does not. Five of seven anchored patterns differ, and one was already under PCRE — the hextet validator. Filed and fixed as RADD-kurxtbqc.

Deliberately **not** done here: swapping the remaining TRE call sites to PCRE. Measured at 1.2x–3x, but every one is anchored, so each needs `\z` and its own differential test. Noted in §11.2.2 rather than bundled in.

| site | TRE | PCRE |
|---|---|---|
| ipv6.R#210 `(^:|::|:$)` | 0.517 | 0.319 |
| ipv6.R#188 `(^:|:$)` | 0.321 | 0.259 |

each needs a differential test over newline/CR/empty/NA input asserting the
PCRE form agrees with the TRE form it replaces.

anchored pattern into a negated character scan plus `nchar()`, worth
0.386 s -> 0.260 s. That is a semantic rewrite of a validator, not an engine
swap, so it wants its own verification -- especially under the leading-zeros
dialect, where validity depends on the significant-digit count rather than
the raw width.

Bounded value: the sites above are roughly a fifth of `addr_parse()`. Section
11.2 stands either way -- this does not bring parse v6 near the 3x target,
and it should be taken for its own sake, not as progress against O1.

**The issue's premise was incomplete.** It said each anchored site needs \z and a differential test, which is right, but PCRE differs from TRE a *second* way: its `.` does not match a newline. Two of the eleven are greedy runs to a final separator (`^.*\.` for a host's last label, `^.*:` for the IPv6 dotted-quad tail) and both needed `(?s)`. Without it `1.2\n.3` keeps its middle part instead of reducing to `3`, and `1\n:2` does not match at all. RADD-kurxtbqc could not have surfaced this: the hextet grammar contains no `.`.

Measured, interleaved passes over both trees at 1e6 distinct addresses, min of 7:

| surface | TRE | PCRE | |
|---|---|---|---|
| addr_strict() v6 | 3.55 s | 3.18 s | -10% |
| addr_pton() v6 | 3.67 s | 3.36 s | -8% |
| addr_strict() v4 | 1.47 s | 1.35 s | -7% |
| ends_in_a_number() | 0.572 s | 0.324 s | **1.8x** |
| addr_whatwg() v4 | 1.30 s | 1.31 s | - |
| addr_aton() v4 | 1.65 s | 1.71 s | - |

The two parse_ipv4_number_slow() sites need a radix prefix to be reached at all. In situ on the 4e6 pieces addr_strict() splits, that one site is 0.159 s TRE vs 0.071 s PCRE (2.2x, matching bench/tokenize.R), and 0.088 s of it is most of the 0.12 s the surface moved.

The negative control does not reproduce RADD-kurxtbqc and that is the interesting part: **no address moves under the naive swap.** What moves is the reason (`1.2.3.4\n` from no code to not_a_number, `::\n` from bad_hextet to empty_group) and ends_in_a_number(), the gate deciding whether a WHATWG host may fall back to a reg-name. Restructure committed as 119259f. Both halves of the issue are now done.

**The hextet validator is a negated scan plus a width, not a regex.** In situ on the 8e6 pieces addr_pton() splits per 1e6 addresses: 0.363 s anchored (strict form), 0.404 s (leading-zero form), **0.214 s** restructured — the scan is 0.144 and the nchar() 0.017. The significant-digit rule is the only surviving regex, and its strip is the same one strtoi() needs, so it runs once and only on pieces wider than a hextet. Side effect: the IPv6 half of the `^0+(.)` TRE site is retired in favour of the verified-equivalent `(?s)^0+(?=.)`. The IPv4 half remains.

| mutation | rows moved |
|---|---|
| strip to empty rather than keeping a digit | 12 |
| borrow integer.R's `^0+(?=[0-9])` lookahead | 9 |
| significant-digit bound off by one | 21 |

| drop the `width == 0L` term | **0** |

**Status:** done | **Parent:** tazdtmvwzachzhvyjfxexfpyhuypyavp

### Description

#### 2026-07-26 — 142225707+bart-turczynski@users.noreply.github.com

Epic F implemented, all five subissues done. R/parse.R is new, 403 tests passing (was 255), lintr clean, R CMD check 0/0/1 (the same private-repo URL NOTE).

RADD-dppkgkmr -- the record. Fields per 5.2, with one thing settled that the table was too compressed to say: `outcome` and `codes` are **data-frame columns**, four each, one per primitive. That is what 'one per primitive' has to mean once it is a vector of the record's own length. The other reading -- a length-four object per row -- allocates four lists per address and puts a per-element loop in the middle of an engine built to avoid one.

RADD-sadkzmde -- the derived status. This is where the work was, and it needed a correction to 5.2 that is now written up as 5.2.1. **`ok` means every primitive with a say accepts, not all four.** Two silences look alike and are not:

  ::1            aton is AF_INET by signature and has no IPv6 grammar to
                 withhold. Counting that as dissent makes EVERY IPv6 address
                 divergent and the print method loud about `::1`.
  1.2.3.4 junk   strict has the IPv4 grammar and declines to see an address --
                 but aton finds 1.2.3.4 in it. Real disagreement, and exactly
                 the class where curl reaches a host a browser will not dial.

So a dialect has a say when it accepted, or when it is applicable (has a grammar for the family the literal is spelled in) and either saw an attempt or some other dialect found an address in the string. An acceptance anywhere means the literal is an address and no applicable dialect gets to shrug after that. 5.2's table says 'all four' because its worked examples are all IPv4, where all four are applicable.

The consequence: aton reports not_an_address on a colon literal, for `::ffff:1.2.3.4` exactly as for `::1`, so the outcome no longer depends on how the tail is spelled.

RADD-ntxlzuit -- addr_reading/addr_outcome/addr_codes, all six dialect names. The compositions resolve from the four stored primitives. One thing that does NOT resolve from the readings alone: getaddrinfo's whitespace gate, which is re-derived from the stored input and carries its own `whitespace` code. The property test asserts addr_reading(p, d) equals dialect_fn(d)(x) for all six over an 18-row corpus, which is the real guarantee that the resolution is faithful.

RADD-lxpdtrje -- print. Quiet on agreement: a column of addresses and nothing else. Loud on divergence: a status tally plus one expanded block per divergent row showing all four readings with their codes, capped at five with '... and N more'. format()/as.character() default to whatwg per section 4.

RADD-wjbscyvu -- vectorized diagnostics. addr_parse() emits no conditions at all; `expect_silent` over 1e4 bad rows. The print report is one status line and at most five blocks however long the vector is. This is the 'refuse ipaddress's diagnostics' half of section 9 correction 6.

Also added and recorded in 6.1: addr_input() and is_raddr_parse(). input is a field the print method shows, so leaving it reachable only via vctrs::field() was a wart.

**Status:** done | **Parent:** vbsszjhsnayjncvmiuelqdfxftibjwri

### Description

Nine corrections the research sweep found in already-shipped work. The provenance one (R/registry.R, architecture.md section 7.1) is already done in 5d207ba; these are the rest.

R/transition.R:
- :125 and architecture.md:1023 say the embedded address 'straddles the reserved u-byte ... so FOUR of the six are split'. It is THREE -- /40, /48, /56. The data tables immediately below both comments already encode three, so the prose contradicts the data it introduces.
- :70-71 asserts RFC 6052 /48 geometry under 64:ff9b:1::/48. RFC 8215 section 5 explicitly forbids assuming 'the existence and location of embedded IPv4 addresses' under that prefix. Epic J would have extracted a confident wrong answer. Also change the citation from section 3 to section 5 (or 3 and 5), since section 5 carries the normative rule.
- :91-92 and :194-195 say Teredo's client address is 'the only complemented field'. The mapped UDP port at bits 80-95 is also XOR 0xFFFF. True only of ADDRESSES, and only because the overlay stores no non-address fields. Restate, and consider carrying the port with a non-IPv4 role so Epic J does not rediscover the complement.
- :45-46 says 'No RFC assigns this' for ::ffff:0:0:0/96. RFC 2765 section 2.1 defined it; RFC 6145 -> RFC 7915 dropped it. Correct wording: 'no CURRENT RFC assigns it'.
- :62 says 192.88.99.0/24 'embeds nothing'. True of the IPv4 side, but 192.88.99.1 has a defined 6to4 image at 2002:c058:6301:: -- a reportable fact.

R/registry.R:
- :38-41 gives ONE shared reason for Teredo's and 6to4's N/A. They have two, with two different IANA footnotes: 6to4 follows the embedded IPv4 (RFC 3056); Teredo's relay advertisement is voluntary and per-deployment (RFC 4380 section 5.4). architecture.md:944-948 and :998-1004 carry the same merged claim. A reader following footnote [2] will not find the stated reason.

docs/architecture.md:
- :902 says 'Globally Reachable IS is_global, authoritatively'. Line 774 already says the opposite ('the IANA column, NOT a derived is_global'), and RFC 8190 section 3 renamed the column from 'Global' precisely to stop that reading. True holds for AS112, AMT, PCP/TURN/SRP anycast, ORCHIDv2 and DETs, none of which is a public host, and ORCHIDs 'should not appear in actual IPv6 headers' at all. Line 902 is the outlier; delete it.
- :173-174 says pton is 'the one platform-dependent dialect'. aton diverges too: glibc's inet_aton ignores trailing garbage so '1.2.3.4junk' SUCCEEDS, musl and Apple reject it. The aton row of section 3.3 needs the same platform caveat the pton row carries.
- :195-198 states the inet_aton trailing-garbage result unqualified; it is Apple-only and there are three different answers.
- :319-322 cites RFC 6874 as live. Obsoleted August 2025 by RFC 9844, which drops the zone-in-URI syntax entirely because browsers found it impracticable. This IMPROVES the existing argument: the recorded measurement 'ada rejects even %25lo0' now has a standards explanation rather than being an observation.

R/dialects.R:
- :196-197's fe80::/10 word bounds 4269801472-4273995775 are unsourced. Attach RFC 4291 section 2.5.6. Note this code models Apple's resolver behaviour deliberately, so it uses the /10 correctly -- the citation is for the bounds, not a conformance claim.

Evidence: docs/research/delta-a-registries.md, delta-b-ranges.md, delta-c-parsers.md.

1. Uniform octets are blind to the hazards this package is built around. Four
   independently drawn octets land on 0x80000000 about once in 10^5, so
   removing widen_word()'s NA guard -- the ipaddress bug of O11(b),
   reintroduced on purpose -- passed every property. Addresses are drawn a WORD
   at a time now, half from a hazard pool, half uniform. That mutation is now
   caught by four properties instead of none, and it also caught a
   trailing-zero renderer that had been surviving on the same blindness
   (an address ending in .0 is a 1-in-256 draw).

2. Transitivity cannot fail while the order goes through a vctrs proxy. A
   lexicographic comparison of proxy columns IS a total order, so no proxy --
   however wrong -- can be intransitive. The first mutation I wrote here
   (compare on one octet) was rejected for exactly that reason: one key still
   gives a transitive relation. So what the property actually guards is
   totality -- comparison answering NA, which is O11(b)'s shape and makes the
   order undefined rather than intransitive -- plus ties being an equivalence.

## RADD-ssschhlu: O11b — file the 0x80000000 equality bug on davidchall/ipaddress

**Status:** done | **Parent:** dtdcaphzgdcnwmnlxjaomoeceuiscggd

### Description

ipaddress 1.0.3 stores address words as R integer. R reserves the bit pattern 0x80000000 (INT_MIN) as NA_integer_, so one address per word position is unrepresentable and silently becomes NA at the R level.

REPRODUCER (verified 2026-07-26, macOS arm64, R 4.6.0, ipaddress 1.0.3):

    library(ipaddress)
    a <- ip_address("0.0.0.128")

    a == a
    #> NA            <- should be TRUE

    is.na(a)
    #> FALSE         <- so it is not reported as missing
    as.character(a)
    #> "0.0.0.128"   <- and it formats correctly
    unclass(a)$address1
    #> NA            <- but the stored word is NA_integer_

Contrast, same package:

    ip_address("128.0.0.0") == ip_address("128.0.0.0")
    #> TRUE          <- fine, because ipaddress stores little-endian

ipaddress stores words LITTLE-endian, so the colliding IPv4 literal is 0.0.0.128 (bytes 00 00 00 80 -> word 0x80000000). Name the byte order whenever quoting a literal: raddr stores big-endian, so raddrs colliding literal is 128.0.0.0. Same defect, different literal.

SCOPE: one IPv4 address. For IPv6 it is every address with that pattern in any of the four words -- roughly 4 x 2^96 addresses, including ordinary-looking ones.

WHY IT MATTERS: the C++ formatter reads the raw bits, so printing and as.character() both look correct. Only comparison fails, and it fails to NA rather than FALSE -- so `if (addr == blocked)` is skipped rather than taken, and any dplyr/base filter silently drops the row.

NOT AN R BUG. R documents the integer range as +/-2147483647 (?integer, .Machine$integer.max), warns on as.integer(-2147483648) with "NAs introduced by coercion to integer range", and states in ?bitwAnd that "pairwise operations can result in integer NA". The in-band NA sentinel is a deliberate, documented design choice inherited from S. The defect is storing unsigned 32-bit data in a signed type with a reserved value and not handling the collision.

SUGGESTED FIX FOR UPSTREAM: either widen the comparison proxy to double (mapping the NA_integer_ pattern back to 2^31), or carry missingness in a separate field so a word reading NA_integer_ is unambiguously the bit pattern. raddr takes the latter approach -- see docs/architecture.md section 5.1.1.

Report at https://github.com/davidchall/ipaddress/issues

### Comments

#### 2026-07-30 — bartek@turczynski.pl

DRAFT COMPLETE, not submitted. _scratch/outbound-drafts/ipaddress-01-equality-int-min.md (gitignored, survives the session). Submission still blocked -- suspension re-verified today, day 10: git ls-remote and gh api user both 403.

Re-measured against ipaddress 1.0.3 / R 4.6.0 rather than reusing the 2026-07-26 numbers. The core reproducer in this issue is EXACT: 0.0.0.128 gives == NA, is.na FALSE, formats correctly, stored word NA. Little-endian confirmed (1.0.0.0 -> word 1; 0.0.0.1 -> 16777216). Four things changed.

1. THE BLAST RADIUS IS NARROWER THAN THIS ISSUE CLAIMS, and that is what produced a better fix. 'Only comparison fails... any dplyr/base filter silently drops the row' is too broad. Measured correct on 0.0.0.128: < > <= >= sort min max, match %in% unique duplicated, is_within, is.na, as.character, + and -. Broken: == and != ONLY. So filter(addr %in% blocklist) is fine; filter(addr == target) and if (addr == blocked) are not.

2. MECHANISM, which the issue did not have. ipaddress ships vec_proxy_compare.ip_address/.ip_network/.ip_interface (8 x 16-bit fields, NA-free -- which is why ordering works) but NO vec_proxy_equal method. Equality falls back to the raw record fields, vec_equal propagates the NA, == returns NA. Confirmed: vec_equal(a,a) NA vs vec_equal(a,a,na_equal=TRUE) TRUE vs vec_match(a,a) 1 vs vec_compare(a,a) 0. match/unique are correct rather than accidentally correct -- a genuinely missing address carries all four words NA PLUS is_ipv6 NA, so it is distinguishable; verified a %in% ip_address(NA) is FALSE and unique(c(a, NA_addr)) has length 2. No conflation is possible.

3. FIX IS ONE METHOD PER CLASS, reusing machinery already in the package: vec_proxy_equal.ip_address <- function(x, ...) vec_proxy_compare(x). Verified live by registering it: == TRUE, != FALSE, cross-address FALSE, ip_address(NA)==ip_address(NA) still NA, match unaffected. Strictly better than this issue's suggestion (widen to double mapping the sentinel to 2^31, or a separate missingness field) -- no storage change, one source of truth for the bit comparison.

4. THE IPv6 LITERALS WERE MISSING AND ARE NOT WHAT YOU'D GUESS. This issue says 'roughly 4 x 2^96 addresses, including ordinary-looking ones' but names none. Because storage is byte-reversed, the colliding 32-bit group is 0x00000080, not 0x80000000 -- i.e. a group written 0:80, so any address ending ::80. Verified NA from ==: ::80, fe80::80, 2001:db8::80, 64:ff9b::80, ::ffff:0.0.0.128, ::80:0:0, 0:0:0:80::. fe80::80 is a plain link-local and 2001:db8::80 is documentation-range. Count refined to 4*2^96 - 6*2^64 + 4*2^32 - 1.

ALSO: scope widens beyond ip_address. ip_network('0.0.0.128/32') == itself and ip_interface('0.0.0.128/32') == itself both return NA. This issue mentioned only ip_address.

Kept this issue's 'NOT AN R BUG' paragraph -- verified the ?integer / ?bitwAnd citations hold. Status returned to todo: drafting is done, but the deliverable is a FILED report and filing cannot start.

## RADD-sytkadrv: Guard defect to file on sitemapr + robotstxtr: a trailing separator defeats the fail-closed posture

**Status:** done | **Parent:** lwjlpzxlmnqghrarwqohqogrsbgqghjm

### Description

Found by RADD-cdmoeadr's migration diff, 2026-07-29. Present in BOTH repos, identically -- R/ssrf.R's IP body is byte-identical across them (232 lines, 11 functions), so this is one defect in two places.

R's strsplit() drops a trailing empty field. strsplit('1:2:3:4:5:6:7:8:', ':') returns EIGHT groups, not nine, so ssrf_expand_zero_run()'s arity check passes and the literal reads as a valid address. The same mechanism makes ssrf_is_dotted_quad('1.2.3.4.') return TRUE.

Affected: '::1:' reads as ::1, '::ffff:' reads as ::ffff and is then decoded as the IPv4-compatible address 0.0.255.255, '1:2:3:4:5:6:7:8:' reads as the full address, '1.2.3.4.' reads as a canonical dotted-quad.

This contradicts the guard's own header, which states the invariant that a literal that cannot resolve to exactly 8 hextets 'is refused with malformed-address rather than reaching the default allow' (SITE-zgufvkks / ROBO-udnyuuwn) -- and independence from rurl's pre-validation is exactly what SITE-vovtwvuh set out to establish.

SEVERITY IS BOUNDED, and should be stated that way when filing. The hole makes the guard read 'X:' as 'X', so it OVER-accepts rather than under-blocks: '::1:' still classifies as loopback and is still refused. What breaks is the documented invariant, not a specific block. No bypass has been demonstrated.

raddr's answer: all three IPv6 forms are 'malformed' under every one of the six dialects. The trailing DOT is different and is NOT a defect -- see the sibling issue.

Fix shape: split with a sentinel, or test the raw literal for a leading/trailing ':' before splitting.

Read-only measurement; nothing was changed in either repo.

### Comments

#### 2026-07-29 — 142225707+bart-turczynski@users.noreply.github.com

FILED. sitemapr SITE-hnbuabqb and robotstxtr ROBO-zavqklmi, both priority medium, cross-linked to each other and back to this issue.

Re-verified read-only against current HEADs first (sitemapr 48280c0, robotstxtr 8ec12ae) — reproduces identically in both:

  ::1:              -> hextets 0000:...:0001  classify = loopback
  ::ffff:           -> hextets 0000:...:ffff  classify = ipv4-compatible, embedded 0.0.255.255
  1:2:3:4:5:6:7:8:  -> hextets 0001:...:0008  classify = NA (allowed)
  ssrf_is_dotted_quad('1.2.3.4.') = TRUE

THREE THINGS THE RE-MEASUREMENT SHARPENED, all carried into the filed reports:

1. The strsplit asymmetry is directional, and that halves the defect surface. R drops a trailing empty field but KEEPS a leading one: strsplit(':1:2:...:8', ':') returns NINE elements, so a leading single colon is ALREADY caught by the arity check. Only the trailing case leaks. The fix note now says leading/trailing rather than implying both are broken.

2. raddr's answer is not 'malformed under all six dialects'. No dialect reads any of the three as an address, but the outcome differs: rejected under strict/whatwg/pton/getaddrinfo/curl, and not_an_address under aton, which has no IPv6 concept. Filed as the two-outcome fact rather than collapsed to one word.

3. The trailing-DOT aside now has its measurement. '1.2.3.4.' is ACCEPTED by whatwg (reads as 1.2.3.4, since the WHATWG host parser drops one trailing empty part) and rejected by the other five. That is exactly why it is not a defect for a guard classifying URL hosts — the guard agrees with WHATWG. Filed as deliberately left alone, with the dialect table as the reason.

CORRECTION to this issue's description: the byte-identical region is 232 code lines and 24 functions, not 11. ## RADD-tazdtmvw: raddr v0.1 — offline IP address parsing and registry-backed classification

**Status:** todo

### Description

Plan issue. Source of truth: _scratch/SPEC.md (draft spec, 2026-07-25), backed by _scratch/BRAINSTORM.md (evidence log) and _scratch/COMPETITORS.md (prior-art survey).

Thesis: one IP literal can have several defensible readings (0177.0.0.1 parses to 127.0.0.1 under inet_aton/WHATWG and 177.0.0.1 under inet_pton). Every existing library picks one and discards the rest. raddr does not pick: it reports every dialect's reading plus a status, and classifies only parsed values against the IANA special-purpose registries.

Scope: pure R, zero I/O, vctrs + rlang only. Deps deliberately minimal.
Out of scope permanently: DNS, HTTP, geolocation, IDNA, URL parsing, allow/deny policy, risk scores, CIDR set algebra.

Publishing order is forced (SPEC 15): ship raddr to CRAN BEFORE rurl/sitemapr/robotstxtr drop their duplicate guards.

### Comments

#### 2026-07-26 — 142225707+bart-turczynski@users.noreply.github.com

Design review complete (2026-07-26). docs/architecture.md now holds the settled design and supersedes _scratch/SPEC.md.

Headline revisions:
- Dialects sit on a paper/reality axis: strict + whatwg (standards), pton + aton (implementations), with getaddrinfo (pton->aton) and curl (aton->pton) as precedence compositions. Six dialects from four primitives.
- Parse outcomes are per-dialect; top-level status is derived. A single scalar could not express 4294967296 (aton accepts it as 0.0.0.0, whatwg rejects as overflow, strict rejects as non-dotted-quad).
- raddr is a shower, not a protector. addr_worst_case() and the cloud-metadata overlay moved to ssrfr. effective_scope -> embedded_scope.
- Six factual errors found in the draft spec, each verified locally.
- New correctness finding: R reserves 0x80000000 as NA_integer_, so the naive 4x int32 layout cannot represent one address per word position. ipaddress 1.0.3 ships this bug. raddr keeps integer storage and widens the comparison proxy to double.

Tree rebuilt against the new model: 14 epics, 65 atomic subissues.

#### 2026-07-28 — 142225707+bart-turczynski@users.noreply.github.com

Measured the raddr<->rurl delta directly (both loaded from source, rurl @ e907017).

WHATWG IPv4: raddr addr_whatwg matches rurl's .parse_whatwg_ipv4_host on 31/31 targeted cases and across a 99-literal sweep. Delegable as-is.

Two things that scope the migration bigger than 'rurl keeps the serializer':

1. rurl's libcurl profile has NO raddr counterpart. parse-web.R is rurl's CURLU
   reproduction (URL-host layer). raddr's addr_curl() is documented as
   'aton, falling back to pton' -- the RESOLVER layer. They are different layers,
   and both are right about their own. Verified against local Apple libc:
   inet_aton('192.0.048.1') REJECTs (048 is not octal), inet_pton accepts it as
   192.0.48.1 decimal -- so addr_curl gives 192.0.48.1, while libcurl's CURLU
   keeps it a reg-name. Delegating rurl's web profile to addr_curl() would
   regress 7/18 sampled hosts (192.0.048.1, 08.0.0.1, 09.1.1.1, 1.2.3.09,
   0Xff, 4294967296, 0x100000000) against rurl's libcurl calibration.
   raddr would need a URL-host-layer curl dialect, or rurl keeps parse-web.R.

2. The host/address boundary must stay in rurl. raddr is an address parser with
   no reg-name concept; rurl's .host_ends_in_number_vec() gate is what keeps
   '0xg', '...', '.', '..' as valid reg-names. Ungated delegation turns those
   into parse failures.

The serializer caveat is real but NOT blocking and is narrower than reported:
the divergence set is exactly ::ffff:0:0/96 (v6_4in6). ::1.2.3.4 and
64:ff9b::1.2.3.4 already agree. A ~20-line WHATWG serializer over the EXPORTED
addr_to_bytes() reproduced rurl's output on 18/18 incl. all compression edge
cases. raddr does not need to grow a WHATWG renderer.

## RADD-tkpqvomv: parse_ipv4_number_slow() is 13% of an IPv6 parse, rejecting literals the fast path could decline sooner

**Status:** done | **Parent:** pbwpleuzfntiksjhkjicnjrgyxkthhqd

### Description

Fell out of O17's profile (RADD-mvtkwncu, 2026-07-29), which was looking for something else and found this instead.

MEASURED: Rprof over 3 runs of 3e5 IPv6 literals, addr_parse() total 9.138 s.
  parse_ipv4_number_slow   1.188 s   13.00%
  parse_ipv4_addr          1.676 s   18.34%  (on IPv6 input)
  parse_ipv6_addr          5.080 s   55.59%

WHY IT FIRES. The IPv4 dialects are family-agnostic and must try every literal in order to reject it. parse_ipv4_number()'s fast path (R/ipv4.R ~75-95) takes only a pure-decimal run of 1-10 digits with no leading zero. An IPv6 literal split on '.' is ONE part -- the whole 39-char colon-bearing string -- which is not decimal, so every IPv6 row declines the fast path and enters the general case.

The general case then does real work before finding out the answer is no: hex-prefix grepl, octal grepl, leading-zero sub(), width/overflow arithmetic against ipv4_max_digits, a truncation substring(), and only then the digit-at-a-time alphabet walk that discovers the ':' and rejects.

THE SHAPE OF A FIX. A part containing any character outside [0-9a-fA-FxX] cannot be a valid IPv4 number under any radix, so one grepl could decline the whole IPv6 corpus before the general case starts. Cheap and, on the face of it, equivalence-preserving.

DO NOT TAKE THAT ON FAITH. This sits on the hottest correctness path in the package and under hedgehog property tests plus helper-slow.R's second implementation. The guard has to be shown equivalent, not argued to be: the empty digit run of a bare '0x' and the status/empty triple that parse_ipv4_number() returns both have corners, and the alphabet is per-radix while the guard would be over their union.

NOT URGENT. addr_parse() has no stated performance target (architecture 11), the engines are already at or under the 4x floor, and 13% of the family that is already the slower one is worth having but is not worth a correctness regression. Do it after O1 (RADD-jyeuyxqs) has said whether the section 11 targets are met at all -- if they are, this is optional.

### Comments

#### 2026-07-29 — 142225707+bart-turczynski@users.noreply.github.com

Decomposed the parse path in a5583e6 looking for another 11.1.7-shaped defect. NULL RESULT: there isn't one. Documented as 11.2.1.

Method: corpora whose real work differs by orders of magnitude, by-line decomposition, looking for a component that refuses to move. First pass used rep() of one literal and was discarded -- R interns strings, so a homogeneous corpus manufactures flatness wherever it looks. Distinct-address corpora, dense lands at 5.63 s against 11.2's independent 5.64 s (calibration).

addr_strict(), 1e6 distinct IPv6, self time by line:

                        dense/8   2001:db8:X::Y/4   ::X/1
  total                  5.63 s        5.12 s      3.20 s
  #229 strsplit          0.69          0.64        0.50
  #230 grepl hextet      0.73          0.71        0.46
  #241 strtoi            0.39          0.46        0.14
  #202 elision expand      --          0.92        0.38

The hextet stage costs the same for 4 input groups as for 8 (1.81 s vs 1.81 s) and the 4-group row pays 0.92 s on top. Flat BY DESIGN: #202 materializes the elided zeros as TEXT, so ::1 becomes 0:0:0:0:0:0:0:1 and every row reaches the validator as 8 groups. On ::X the regex checks 8e6 pieces of which 7e6 are zeros the code wrote itself one line earlier.

So elision is a surcharge, not a saving -- the compact form costs more per input group than the expanded one.

Bounds on the available wins:
- not materializing the zeros: ~35% on the elided corpus, 1.55x, parse v6 41x -> ~26x
- distinct-value trick on the hextet regex (11.1.1's): 2.1x-3.7x on #230, NOTHING on #241 where match() costs what strtoi() did. ~14% of the call.

RECOMMENDATION ON THIS ISSUE. The 13% here is the same order as both of the above, and stacking all three still leaves parse v6 an order of magnitude past a 3x target. The guard sits on the hottest correctness path in the package -- hedgehog properties, helper-slow.R's second implementation, the bare-0x empty digit run, per-radix alphabets vs a union guard -- and 11.2's floor conclusion (now better evidenced) says compiled code in v0.2 makes all three irrelevant. I'd close this as won't-do on that evidence rather than spend the risk, but leaving it in-progress for your call since the issue predates the floor being this well established.

Why this is a null result and 11.1.7 was not, since both were reached the same way: extract_embeddings() did work proportional to n for a result proportional to the embeddings, and a complexity mismatch is a bug at any constant. The parser does work proportional to 8 groups for a result proportional to 8 groups -- it just reaches 8 sooner than it must. Constant factor, and constant factors on irregular string work are the pure R floor.

Verify gate green.

#### 2026-07-29 — 142225707+bart-turczynski@users.noreply.github.com

CLOSED WON'T-DO, by user decision 2026-07-29, on the evidence in 11.2.1 (commit a5583e6).

No status for won't-do exists in this project (todo / in-progress / done only), so this is marked done. Nothing was implemented. The union-alphabet pre-filter described in the issue body was never written.

Rationale, restated so a future reader does not take 'done' for 'shipped':

Done in 9a8a91d. Title stays stale on purpose -- there is no embedded_scope and no scalar accessor; addr_embeddings() always returns the typed list.

What landed:
  - the recursion: category is the classification of the EXTRACTED address, one level of addr_classify() per row. Terminates by construction, not by a depth guard -- an extracted address is IPv4, the only IPv4 overlay row is 192.88.99.0/24, and that prefix has no geometry, so the inner call finds no kind.   - the two MUST-drop codes plus Teredo's conditional MUST. All eight classify codes now fire; test-codes.R names one input per code instead of carrying a pending list.

Those two records must differ -- the outer one is an IPv6 address in ::ffff:0:0/96, and collapsing them is the SSRF class itself. CVE-2024-24790 is caught by the weaker, true statement: the EMBEDDED address classifies as the address it is. Checked over every IPv4 block the category map covers, through both ::ffff: and the deprecated ::, plus four textual spellings of one 128-bit value.

One design decision worth flagging, written up as architecture.md 5.2.4: the 'is the embedded address global' predicate is THREE-valued. Measured over all 256 IPv4 /8s, exactly one block leaves the question open -- 192.88.99.0/24, withdrawn by IANA with no policy at all -- so 2002:c058:6301:: draws no MUST-drop. Asserting one would be reading IANA's N/A as FALSE one level down.

Also recorded: RFC 7050 constructs 64:ff9b::192.0.0.170 and argues its well-known addresses are not among those RFC 5735 section 3 lists. RFC 5735 section 3 does list 192.0.0.0/24, and IANA marks 192.0.0.170/32 Globally Reachable = False. raddr fires the code and leaves the disagreement visible.

## RADD-uvddposi: Pin the 0.1.0 release artifact: build, checksum, and keep the check log

**Status:** todo | **Parent:** rzdchzcswdehavskhjvpmqoqxodvmooy

### Description

Today 0.1.0 is a git tag plus a check that passed once in a terminal. No tarball has been built and kept, and no checksum records what was checked. When the suspension lifts and a submission happens, there will be nothing to prove the submitted artifact is the one that was verified.

The tag itself is sound and does not need to move: v0.1.0 is annotated, points at 7fc7b8b, and every commit since then touches only Rbuildignored paths (docs, data-raw, .github, AGENTS.md), so the built package is byte-identical to the tagged tree. That is worth asserting mechanically rather than by argument, which is part of this issue.

DELIVERABLES.
1. R CMD build, producing raddr_0.1.0.tar.gz.
2. A checksum of the tarball, recorded in a committed file.
3. The passing R CMD check --as-cran log, kept alongside cran-comments.md.
4. A check that building from the v0.1.0 tag and from current HEAD yields the same tarball contents, which pins the claim that only ignored paths have changed since the tag.

NOTE ON WHERE THINGS GO. .gitignore carries *.tar.gz and .Rbuildignore carries ^.*\.tar\.gz$ and ^cran-comments\.md$ and ^CRAN-SUBMISSION$. So the tarball itself must not be committed. What gets committed is the checksum and the log, and they need a home that does not reach R CMD check. docs/ is already ^docs$-ignored and is the obvious candidate.

CAVEAT ON REPRODUCIBILITY, which should be stated in whatever file is committed rather than discovered later: R CMD build embeds a Packaged: timestamp in DESCRIPTION, so two builds of the same tree do not produce identical bytes. The checksum pins one artifact, not a reproducible build. Compare extracted contents, not tarball checksums, when checking the tag against HEAD.

Without it the five policy logicals carry two different NAs a caller cannot tell apart: IANA's own N/A, which it DECLINED to state, and 'that registry has no policy columns at all'. 192.88.99.1 and 8.8.8.8 both classify all-NA and are not the same fact -- merging them is the same mistake as reading N/A as FALSE, one level up. It also makes the per-row registry_version honest, since 7.3 stamped the two pairs separately precisely so one date could not assert something about a table it says nothing about.

2. 'codes', typed and empty, per the 2026-07-27 comment on this issue.

THE SURVEY CHANGED THE ARGUMENT AGAIN (measured live, not quoted from docs/research/). Python netaddr is the only comparable tool that consults more than one registry, and it keys .info BY REGISTRY -- IPv4 / IPv6 / Multicast / IPv6_unicast. Same conclusion, different route. It also has NO special-purpose registry at all, so 192.0.0.9 comes back as '192/8 Administered by ARIN, Legacy' with the globally-reachable carve-out invisible, and 64:ff9b::a9fe:a9fe as '::/8 Reserved by IETF', losing both the registry's Globally Reachable = True and the embedded 169.254.169.254. That is P9's CVE-producing pattern in a FOURTH library. CPython ipaddress and R ipaddress carry no provenance at all -- no block, no RFC, no registry accessor -- and both report is_global AND is_reserved as true for that same address. Provenance is what makes a contradiction inspectable rather than merely present.

embedded_kind is affirmative only (section 5.3.7), with three mechanical rules:
  - a prefix with no geometry is not a kind, so the vocabulary is DERIVED from the geometry table and 6to4_relay_anycast falls out of it. Nothing is embedded IN 192.88.99.0/24; the 6to4 image of 192.88.99.1 is a mapping OUT.
  - ::/96 keeps the tail32 > 1 carve-out, so :: and ::1 are not read as an embedded 0.0.0.0 and 0.0.0.1. Registry fact, not heuristic, and both shipped in-house guards already use it.
  - a prefix outranks the ISATAP interface identifier, which RFC 5214 section 6.1 lets sit under ANY /64. 2002:c000:201:0:0:5efe:1.2.3.4 is 6to4.
ISATAP is matched by comparison against isatap_iid$permitted, never bitwAnd -- w3 can hold 0x80000000.

The matcher is generalized to any prefix table and memoized per table, so the overlay is matched by the same no-bitwise containment as the registries. registry_match() stays as the special-purpose name; the new entry point is prefix_match(x, which).

addr_classify() refuses a raddr_parse as well as a string. Four readings may be four different addresses, and section 4 puts that choice in a function name -- format() may default to whatwg because R structurally forces one value out of it; addr_classify() is not forced.

MEASURED WHILE BUILDING: 8000::/3 is the second 0x80000000 block and it classifies (unallocated), which the totality test would have missed had the matcher used bit operations -- it is an eighth of the IPv6 space, not a /48.

NOT DONE HERE, and it is Epic J (RADD-hffsyrsm): extraction. embeddings is typed, size-stable and one ptype across the vector, with zero rows per element until the extractor lands.

#### 2026-07-27 — 142225707+bart-turczynski@users.noreply.github.com

FOLLOW-UP 765cb29: the record now discloses WHY each of its NAs is NA.

The rule, from the user: be perfectly compliant with a given standard, report everything we know, and where we know two NAs mean different things, disclose it. 'registry' was the first application of it; measuring the rest found the record still merged three reasons into a bare NA.

MEASURED: exactly four special-purpose blocks have a missing policy value, carrying three different reasons.
  192.88.99.0/24  all five NA   deprecated             termination_date 2015-03
  2001:10::/28    all five NA   deprecated (ORCHID)    termination_date 2014-03
  2001::/32       reach only    voluntary relay adv    footnote [2]
  2002::/16       reach only    embedded v4 decides    footnote [3]

The last two are the pair section 7.1 already splits in four places. Both came out of the record as an indistinguishable NA, so raddr_class was quietly becoming the FIFTH place they were merged. Both explaining columns existed in the vendored data and both had been dropped.

'footnotes' does the same job for rfc, which is NA for all 256 IPv4 address-space rows because that registry has no reference column. 42 of the 256 carry a footnote marker and 214 do not -- 'no citation' and 'a citation whose text is on the registry page rather than in the CSV' are different facts. 127.0.0.0/8's [7] is the evidence for the second. Footnote numbering is per registry, so a marker is only interpretable alongside 'registry'.

WHERE THE RULE STOPS, recorded in section 5.3.6 so it is not read as a licence to annotate every absence: embedded_kind = NA also has three causes (no prefix matched; a prefix with no geometry matched; the ::/96 carve-out fired) and gets NO field, because none of them is unrecoverable -- block, name and category sit in the same record and addr_transition_registry() is public and keyed on the block. The record does not duplicate the source tables either: block + registry is an exact key into them, so status, date, notes and allocation_date stay one lookup away. Disclose what only the SOURCE knows.

Present on 3.9.6, 3.12.13 and 3.14.6 [verified 2026-07-27]. _explode_shorthand_ip_string() re-parses str(self) without splitting the scope off first. SCOPE IS MATERIALLY WIDER THAN THIS ISSUE RECORDED. Three classes accept a scope and behave three different ways on .exploded:
  IPv6Address('fe80::1%lo0')       -> raises
  IPv6Network('fe80::%lo0/64')     -> raises
  IPv6Interface('fe80::1%lo0/64')  -> SUCCEEDS, silently dropping the scope
All three keep the scope in .compressed. The Interface escapes only because line 1870 uses str(self.ip) and .ip has already lost the zone. THE FIX IS SIMPLER THAN THIS ISSUE STATES. The diagnosis here -- re-parses str(self) without splitting the scope off -- is correct, but the sharper point is that the re-parse is UNNECESSARY: the integer is already on the object as self._ip. Replacing the round-trip with '%032x' % self._ip was verified on fe80::1%lo0, fe80::1, ::ffff:1.2.3.4%eth0 and 2001:db8::80%1. A _split_scope_id() static helper also already exists in the same class 19 lines below the bug (line 1891, 3.14.6), so an in-file alternative exists too. Checked that it reproduces with NO scope involved, so it is an independent defect; the draft offers to file it separately rather than folding it in and muddying this report.

Line citations are 3.14.6-specific and will drift across versions, so the draft quotes the code rather than leaning on numbers.

## RADD-vpoupbus: The RFC 6052 reserved u-byte is never checked on an address

**Status:** done

### Description

RFC 6052 section 2.2 reserves bits 64-71 and says they MUST be set to zero. raddr's geometry SKIPS those bits, so every extraction is correct whatever they hold -- but a non-zero u-byte is a violation raddr observes and does not report, uniformly across nat64_wk, nat64_local and the new addr_nat64_embeddings().

Evidence it was never wired up: the constant `nat64_u_byte` has sat in R/transition.R since the overlay landed with no consumer at all. RADD-khefauzg gave it its first one, and only for the /96 case where the u-byte falls inside the caller's prefix and is therefore a statement about their configuration rather than about the address.

This is a code-layer change, not a per-function one: a new entry in addr_codes_registry() at `must` strength, emitted from classify wherever a NAT64 geometry was read. Doing it inside one extraction function would have made the same violation reportable under a configured prefix and silent under the well-known one.

Not urgent -- no extraction is wrong today -- but it is a MUST raddr can see and does not say, which is the shape of thing this package exists to not do.

Written up as docs/architecture.md section 5.3.7.2 [open].

### Comments

#### 2026-07-31 — bartek@turczynski.pl

Done in 7fc7b8b -- pulled into 0.1.0 rather than deferred, since it was the one open item between here and a first submission.

nat64_u_byte_nonzero, classify layer, must strength, RFC 6052 section 2.2. Reports a malformed container rather than a wrong reading: section 2.3 says to remove the u octet before reading the embedded address, which the two-segment geometry at /40, /48 and /56 already did, so no extraction changes. Verified directly -- 64:ff9b:1:c000:ff02:2100:: and 64:ff9b:1:c000:2:2100:: both extract 192.0.2.33, and only the first draws the code.

Narrower than the issue assumed. Only nat64_local can reach the rule: under 64:ff9b::/96 the reserved octet falls INSIDE the prefix and is zero by construction, which the tests assert over all 65,536 combinations of the two trailing hextets rather than argue. The emission condition is still written over both kinds, so a prefix added later at another length cannot slip through unreported.

The issue said 'uniform across all three routes'. It is uniform across the two classification routes, and addr_nat64_embeddings() deliberately stays out -- it emits no codes at all, because a caller-supplied prefix produces a reading and codes are a property of a classification. That is section 5.3.7.1's existing boundary, not a new exception; documented in the function's help and in 5.3.7.2.

Also wired into the guards that would catch a future drift: the pinned strength table and the one-literal-per-code corpus in test-codes.R, and the bidirectional reason-code table check against docs/architecture.md. The edge-cases vignette now derives the code count from the registry instead of transcribing 23.




## RADD-vppmbsia: addr_reading(p, "curl") silently corrupts the record under vctrs < 0.7.0

**Status:** done | **Parent:** tazdtmvwzachzhvyjfxexfpyhuypyavp

### Description

CONFIRMED 2026-07-31, and it is NOT an R 4.0 issue. Found while measuring the R 4.0 floor (RADD-dcquzofl), which is why it looked R-version-specific at first. It is not: the variable is the vctrs version.

THE BUG. vctrs < 0.7.0 modifies vctrs_rcrd types IN PLACE in vec_assign(), rather than returning a modified copy. Fixed upstream in vctrs 0.7.0: "vec_assign() no longer modifies POSIXlt and vctrs_rcrd types in place (#1951)".

raddr_address IS a vctrs_rcrd, and raddr calls vec_assign() on one in two places:

  blank_address()    R/parse.R:339   vec_assign(a, at, vec_slice(a, NA_integer_))
  compose_dialects() R/dialects.R:193 vec_assign(first, missing, vec_slice(second, missing))

composed_reading() (R/parse.R:342) computes the gated getaddrinfo reading FIRST, through blank_address(field(x, "aton"), gated), and only then evaluates the curl branch as compose_dialects(field(x, "aton"), gai). Under vctrs < 0.7.0 the first call blanks the record own stored aton field in place, so the second call sees NA and falls through to the gai reading, which is also NA.

OBSERVED, on R 4.0.0 + vctrs 0.6.5, x <- "1.2.3.4 junk":

  addr_aton(x)                    1.2.3.4     addr_reading(p, "aton")     1.2.3.4
  addr_curl(x)                    1.2.3.4     addr_reading(p, "curl")     NA   <- diverges

WORSE THAN A WRONG RETURN VALUE: the corruption PERSISTS in the record. Reading curl poisons p for every later read.

  p <- addr_parse("1.2.3.4 junk")
  addr_reading(p, "curl")    NA
  addr_reading(p, "aton")    NA    <- was 1.2.3.4 before the curl read

So the observable behaviour of a raddr_parse vector depends on the ORDER in which its accessors are called. That breaks the record path equals direct path invariant asserted at tests/testthat/test-invariants.R:269, and it is six of the seven failures in the R 4.0.0 --as-cran run recorded in docs/r-floor-check.md.

MEASURED 2x2, holding one variable at a time. The plain vctrs reproducer needs no raddr at all:
  r <- vctrs::new_rcrd(list(v = c(10L, 20L, 30L)))
  q <- vctrs::vec_assign(r, 2L, vctrs::vec_slice(r, NA_integer_))
  vctrs::field(r, "v")   # 10 NA 30 under vctrs 0.6.5; 10 20 30 under 0.7.3

  R 4.0.0 + vctrs 0.6.5   MUTATED
  R 4.4.2 + vctrs 0.6.5   MUTATED
  R 4.4.2 + vctrs 0.7.3   intact
  R 4.6.0 + vctrs 0.7.3   intact

WHY THIS IS NOT A FLOOR FOOTNOTE, and why it is high priority. DESCRIPTION declares Imports: vctrs with NO version floor. vctrs 0.6.5 was the CURRENT CRAN release from 2023-12-02 to 2026-01-16 - the entire development span of raddr 0.1.0 - so it is what a large share of installed bases still carry. Every one of them gets silent wrong answers and a corrupted record on a supported code path, on any R version. The only reason raddr development never saw it is that this host has vctrs 0.7.3.

raddr code was not wrong: vec_assign() is documented to return a modified copy, and 0.6.5 violated that. So the minimal honest fix is a version floor, Imports: vctrs (>= 0.7.0), NOT a defensive copy that would outlive the upstream bug forever. vctrs 0.7.0 itself declares R (>= 4.0.0), so this floor does not force the R floor up.

ACCEPTANCE
1. DESCRIPTION declares vctrs (>= 0.7.0), with the reason recorded where a reader will find it rather than in a commit message alone.
2. A regression test asserts NON-MUTATION directly - that addr_reading(p, "curl") leaves p unchanged - since the existing invariant test catches the symptom but nothing pins the cause. Note this new assertion passes on a fixed vctrs and so cannot itself be version-gated; it is there to fail loudly if the pattern is reintroduced.
3. Re-run data-raw/check-r-floor.sh with the floor in place and confirm the six failures go away, which is also what unblocks RADD-dcquzofl.

### Comments

#### 2026-07-31 — bartek@turczynski.pl

FIXED and committed as 99e9e05, on branch chore/o12-row-disposition.

DESCRIPTION now declares Imports: vctrs (>= 0.7.0). blank_address() (R/parse.R) carries the reason in a comment at the call site, since the floor on its own explains nothing to a reader.

Two regression tests in tests/testthat/test-invariants.R, because the pre-existing invariant caught the symptom and nothing pinned the cause:

- "reading a dialect does not modify the record it read from" - asserts the record is identical() after each read. Compares against an INDEPENDENTLY parsed record rather than a saved snapshot of p own fields: an in-place write is visible through every reference to the vector it mutates, so a before snapshot taken from p would itself be changed by the thing it is supposed to detect. That is not hypothetical, it is what my first probe did, and it is why the probe printed "input r$v before: 10 NA 30".
- "dialect readings do not depend on the order they are read in" - the user-visible symptom, over all six dialects in both directions rather than the one pair that broke.

VERIFIED IN BOTH DIRECTIONS, which matters because a regression test that cannot fail is decoration:

- Host, R 4.6.0 + vctrs 0.7.3: full gate green, 0 errors 0 warnings 1 NOTE (the expected New submission plus the two 404 GitHub URLs).
- R 4.0.0 + vctrs 0.6.5 with the floor stripped so INSTALL proceeds: both new tests FAIL (test-invariants.R: 7 failed, 238 passed; the two new tests contribute 2 failures each, and the pre-existing record-path invariant the other 3).
- R 4.0.0 + vctrs 0.6.5 with the floor in place: R CMD INSTALL refuses outright - "namespace vctrs 0.6.5 is being loaded, but >= 0.7.0 is required". So the floor is load-bearing, not decorative.

Acceptance criteria 1 and 2 are met. Criterion 3, the re-run of data-raw/check-r-floor.sh against a fixed vctrs, is in progress and reported under RADD-dcquzofl since it is also that issue gate.

#### 2026-07-31 — bartek@turczynski.pl

Blast radius, audited rather than assumed. Four vec_assign() call sites in R/:

- R/parse.R:349  blank_address()      AFFECTED - receives field(x, "aton") / field(x, "pton")
- R/dialects.R:198 compose_dialects() AFFECTED - receives field(x, "aton") via composed_reading()
- R/parse.R:298  readings_agree()     safe - first comes from vec_slice(), a fresh object
- R/ipv4.R:466   parse_dialect_full() safe - out comes from ipv4_address(parsed), freshly built

So only the two composition sites ever received a caller-owned object, and only through composed_reading(). That matches the observed shape exactly: the two new invariant tests fail on precisely 2 of 6 dialects each, getaddrinfo and curl, and the four primitives are untouched because they are plain field() reads with no vec_assign in the path.

Worth being precise about whose object got corrupted, since "mutates its input" could mean something worse than it does. No exported function mutated an argument the user passed in - addr_getaddrinfo() and addr_curl() build their operands fresh, so the direct dialect path was always correct, which is why addr_curl(x) kept returning 1.2.3.4 throughout. What got corrupted was the vector stored INSIDE the raddr_parse record, reached through field(). That is still the user object p and still user-visible, just via later reads of p rather than via the argument.

#### 2026-07-31 — bartek@turczynski.pl

Acceptance criterion 3 met, so this closes. a1aa378 re-ran data-raw/check-r-floor.sh against vctrs 0.7.2 on R 4.0.0: Status OK, 0 errors, 0 warnings, 0 notes. All six curl failures are gone, and the seventh (unrelated, testthat) went with 6eccdcc.

Full state: DESCRIPTION declares vctrs (>= 0.7.0); blank_address() carries the reason at the call site; two non-mutation invariants in test-invariants.R, verified to fail on vctrs 0.6.5 and pass on 0.7.2/0.7.3; R CMD INSTALL refuses outright on 0.6.5.

Not filing upstream. The bug is already fixed in vctrs 0.7.0 (#1951), so there is nothing to report - this was raddr missing a floor, not vctrs missing a fix. Unrelated to RADD-dtdcaphz.

## RADD-wglsdrmu: Codes: add a normative strength column and the classify layer

**Status:** done | **Parent:** vbsszjhsnayjncvmiuelqdfxftibjwri

### Description

Two changes to R/codes.R, settled with the user 2026-07-27.

1. Add a 'strength' column recording the normative force of the rule a code reports: must / should / may / unspecified. NA for the 15 existing parse-layer codes -- those describe what a parser DID, not what a spec mandates, and NA is the honest value rather than a filler.

The user's framing, which corrected an earlier proposal to ship only MUST rules and defer the rest: 'must is must; other language should be reported, but no consequences are needed.' Shipping only the MUSTs would collapse a spectrum into a binary, which is the move raddr exists to refuse. Report all of them and grade them.

2. Add layer = 'classify' codes. The machinery already anticipates this: R/codes.R:96 reads parse_code_levels <- raddr_codes$code[raddr_codes$layer == 'parse'], so the layer column was built to hold more than one value.

The six rules, with strength:

- MUST, consequence defined: the NAT64 Well-Known Prefix 64:ff9b::/96 MUST NOT carry a non-global IPv4 address and translators MUST drop such packets (RFC 6052 section 3.1).
- MUST, consequence defined: 6to4 traffic embedding a V4ADDR that is not global unicast MUST be silently discarded (RFC 3056 section 9).
- MUST, format mandate, no drop rule: only fe80::/64 is well-formed; febf::1 matches the fe80::/10 registry row but is not a valid link-local address (RFC 4291 section 2.5.6).
- MUST NOT, binds the host not the packet: 169.254.0.0/24 and 169.254.255.0/24 MUST NOT be selected by autoconfiguration (RFC 3927 section 2.1).
- Conditional: a Teredo GLOBAL address MUST embed a global-scope client IPv4, while a link-local one MAY embed a private one (RFC 4380 section 4).
- Unspecified, not a violation: fc00::/8 (L=0, centrally assigned) has no defining specification; only fd00::/8 is defined (RFC 4193 section 3.1).

Sequencing: the two MUST-drop codes require extracting and classifying the embedded IPv4, so their VALUES are blocked on Epic J. The vocabulary and the strength column land here; fe80::/64 and fc00::/8 are computable from the prefix alone and can be exercised immediately.

Adding a code is an API addition and removing one is breaking -- that is what 'since' is for, and these are a cross-repo contract with ssrfr on the same footing as the parse codes.

### Comments

#### 2026-07-27 — 142225707+bart-turczynski@users.noreply.github.com

The nearest candidate (RFC 6052 s3.1's SHOULD NOT on constructing IPv4-translatable addresses) is not decidable from an address.

**Measured, and it changed two grades.** I fetched the seven RFC texts rather than trusting the transcriptions. RFC 4291 and RFC 8215 invoke RFC 2119 *nowhere*; RFC 3056, 3927, 4193, 4380 and 6052 all do. So the grade follows the rule's substance, not keyword presence:

- `ula_l_bit_unset` is `unspecified` even though RFC 4193 *does* invoke 2119: s3.1's 'Set to 0 may be defined in the future' is lowercase and nothing ever defined it. Keyword presence in a document says nothing about the sentence that matters.

## RADD-wtwolrzy: Encoding round-trip pairs

**Status:** done | **Parent:** wysgbyngiykiivctaqnhmghrzlaxophi

### Description

addr_to_bytes/binary/hex and their inverses, following ipaddress's symmetric-pair convention.

### Comments

#### 2026-07-27 — 142225707+bart-turczynski@users.noreply.github.com

Done in 13ebb5a. Three symmetric pairs in R/encoding.R following ipaddress's naming (addr_to_bytes/bytes_to_addr and friends).

Design, written up as architecture 6.5.1:
- The width is the family, never the bits. 4 octets for IPv4, 16 for both IPv6 families. This is what keeps 192.0.2.1, ::ffff:192.0.2.1 and the deprecated ::192.0.2.1 apart -- research 08 round-trip failure 2. The 4-in-6 form encodes to 16 octets, not the 4 it embeds (gotcha 23).
- Leading zeros are load-bearing, the opposite of RFC 5952 4.1. Fixed width always; any other width decodes to NA rather than being padded to the nearest one.
- Input leniency is exactly three named things: uppercase hex (RFC 3596 2.5 and RFC 2874 2.2.1 print uppercase), an optional 0x read and never written, and whitespace grouping. Nothing else.
- bytes_to_addr() refuses a bare raw vector: eight octets are one malformed address or two IPv4 addresses.
- The zone does not survive, but == still holds, because 5.1.2 keeps the zone out of equality. Both claims are true and the tests keep them apart.

Tests (78 new, 1073 total): test-encoding.R is organized by research 08's numbered round-trip failures, one section each. Plus a seeded 500-address random-word round trip per pair, which is what would catch an offset that is wrong by one byte in string_word() -- a hand-picked corpus would not.

Measured, architecture 11.1.2, best of seven at 1e6 via bench/record.R (new encoding block): 8 of 12 operations inside the 3x target. bytes_to_addr BEATS the C++ baseline (0.72x/0.92x) and addr_to_bytes is the worst in the table (3.77x/4.02x) -- one cause, the list_of<raw> allocation bound, paid on the way out by us and on the way in by both. binary_to_addr misses at ~4.2x, regex-bound. perl=TRUE on the validity scan was worth 7x (0.99s -> 0.13s) and is the difference between 13x and 4x; the scan cannot be dropped because strtoi() accepts a sign and a 0x prefix, so "0x0000c0" would decode to a real address.

#### 2026-07-29 — 142225707+bart-turczynski@users.noreply.github.com

Settled 2026-07-29, commit d26fc63. Docker probe: debian:bookworm-slim (glibc 2.36) and alpine:3.20 (musl 1.2.5), same two Python oracles, four fixtures committed.

pton: glibc and musl REJECT the leading zeros Apple reads as decimal -- 0177.0.0.1, 192.0.010.1, 192.0.048.1, 10.048.1.1, 00000000177.0.0.1, 0000000000000000001.0.0.1, 010.010.010.010, 0.0.0.010, 0177.0.0.01, plus the IPv6 hextet and dotted-quad-tail equivalents. Not a different reading -- a rejection. So ipaddress's 0177.0.0.1 -> 177.0.0.1 does NOT reproduce on Linux.

The item's own premise was BACKWARDS and is retracted in the doc. It held that glibc 'ignores trailing garbage outright' so 1.2.3.4x succeeds there while 'Apple and musl reject it'. Measured: glibc rejects 1.2.3.4x exactly as Apple does, and accepts 1.2.3.4 x / 127.0.0.1 junk exactly as Apple does. musl is the outlier and it is STRICT -- it refuses even a bare trailing space. Whitespace is the whole of the glibc/musl difference; they are byte-identical on IPv6.

The finding worth the most is the negative one: section 3.2's composition is platform-STABLE. getaddrinfo = pton-then-aton behind the same whitespace pre-step on all three libcs, on all 91 IPv4 rows, with the same ten gate rows on Apple and glibc (invisible on musl only because its aton rejected them first). Every primitive varies; the algebra over them does not.

No code change. raddr models Apple and must, per P1.

## RADD-ybhyvkhk: Epic D — IPv6 parsing

**Status:** done | **Parent:** tazdtmvwzachzhvyjfxexfpyhuypyavp

### Description

The genuinely new work. :: elision, dotted-quad tail, zone into its own field.

### Comments

#### 2026-07-26 — 142225707+bart-turczynski@users.noreply.github.com

Epic D landed on branch feature/ipv6-parsing (commit e10f98c). All three subissues done. 216 tests (was 133), lintr clean, R CMD check 0/0/1.

R/ipv6.R is one vectorized engine and two rule sets, wired into the six existing dialects via parse_dialect(x, rules, rules6) rather than added beside them. It rewrites each literal to its expanded eight-hextet form as text, then parses 8n hextets in one flat pass.

New oracle: data-raw/oracle-ipv6.py and .R, 126 rows, covering Apple inet_pton / inet_aton / getaddrinfo, Python ipaddress and ada. Findings now in docs/architecture.md section 3.5:

- The disagreement inverts. strict and whatwg diverge on six of the eight IPv4 rows; about IPv6 they agree on every measured input.
- inet_pton has no width limit on hextet leading zeros, then caps significant digits at four.
- getaddrinfo lifts the second hextet of fe80::/10 into the scope ID and clears it, zone or no zone. fe80:abcd::1 is fe80::1%43981 to getaddrinfo and unchanged to inet_pton. That is the IPv6 headline row.
- inet_pton runs the same convention forwards. raddr does not reproduce that fold (if_nametoindex reads the host interface table, so it is not a function of the input) and does reproduce the lift (which is).
- The dotted-quad tail is the dialect's own IPv4 rule set, so whatwg's IPv6 tail is stricter than whatwg's standalone IPv4 parser.
- getaddrinfo's whitespace gate covers the address, not the zone.

Decision recorded in 3.5.2: strict rejects the zone ID. Python and Go accept, Rust does not, so the named references do not decide it; RFC 4291's grammar does.

New open items: O13 (curl's IPv6 composition unverified against real curl -- now testable, since pton and getaddrinfo disagree) and O14 (getaddrinfo truncates a numeric zone mod 2^16). O7 closed.

BLOCKED ON PUSH: 'git push' returns 403, 'Your account is suspended'. The commit is local on feature/ipv6-parsing; the verify gate passes locally.
